lessons.title: What Commerce Is
lessons.objective: Define commerce, separate trade from the aids to trade, and distinguish commerce from economics and industry.

content.heading: Commerce
paragraphs: Commerce is the organised exchange of goods and services, plus the services that make exchange possible. It moves goods from producers to consumers without producing them itself.

content.heading: A yam travels to market
paragraphs: A farmer harvests yam in Benue and sells it to a trader. The trader hires a lorry, stores the yam in a warehouse, insures the stock and pays through a bank. By the time the yam reaches a Lagos market, several people have earned money without growing anything.

Commerce is the branch of production that moves goods and services from producers to consumers. It begins where production ends. Trade is the buying and selling itself: home trade inside a country, foreign trade across borders. Aids to trade are the services that support exchange, such as transport, warehousing, banking, insurance, advertising and communication.
bullets: Trade is the exchange act; aids to trade make exchange possible.
Commerce creates place, time and possession utility.
content.takeaway: Commerce moves goods and services; it does not create them.

check.question: Which activity is trade rather than an aid to trade?
options: A bank lending money to a trader
A shop buying goods to resell
A lorry carrying goods to market
check.why: Trade is buying and selling; the others are services that support it.

visual.caption: Commerce carries the yam from producer to consumer; each link adds a service, not another good.

content.heading: Why a trader is not a manufacturer
paragraphs: A cement factory turns limestone into cement. A construction firm uses the cement to build a road. A trader buys the cement and resells it to the firm. All three are useful, but only the first two produce goods.

Commerce is often confused with economics and industry. Economics studies how scarce resources are allocated. Industry studies production itself: extraction, manufacturing and construction. Commerce studies the institutions and services that carry out exchange. A question that names farming, mining or manufacturing is pointing at production, not commerce.
bullets: Industry produces; commerce distributes and supports.
Economics explains allocation; commerce explains exchange institutions.
content.takeaway: If the work creates a good it is production; if it moves or supports the sale it is commerce.

check.question: A company mines tin and sells the ore to a factory. What is the mining?
options: Trade, because the ore is sold
An aid to trade, because a sale happens
Industry, because it takes a raw material from nature
Commerce, because the ore changes hands
check.why: Mining is extractive production; the sale does not turn it into commerce.

content.heading: What commerce does
paragraphs: Commerce performs several functions at once. It exchanges goods, distributes them, stores them until demand appears, finances trade, spreads risk and supplies information about prices and products. Without these functions, goods would sit where they are made and buyers would not know they exist.

It also creates employment and widens consumer choice by making more goods available. Advertising and communication tell buyers what exists and where to find it. Each link in the chain earns its margin by adding a service.
bullets: Exchange, distribution and storage move goods to the buyer.
Banking finances trade; insurance spreads its risk.
Advertising informs buyers; transport and communication connect markets.
Commerce widens consumer choice by making more goods available.
content.takeaway: Commerce coordinates the chain from producer to consumer.

check.question: Which function of commerce is performed by insurance?
options: It spreads the risk of loss.
It stores goods until demand appears.
check.why: Insurance does not move or store goods; it shares the cost of possible loss.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: An aid to trade supports buying and selling but is not trade itself. Insurance, transport and banking are aids; the actual exchange of goods is trade.

content.problem: Which of these is an aid to trade? A. Mining B. Insurance C. Farming D. Manufacturing

steps.reason: Trade is buying and selling; an aid makes it possible.
steps.result: Look for a service, not a producer of goods.
steps.predictPrompt: Which option does not create a physical good?

steps.reason: Mining, farming and manufacturing produce goods; insurance covers risk in transit and storage.
Production creates goods; commerce moves and supports them.

content.heading: Go deeper: Commerce, economics and industry — where the boundaries lie
paragraphs: The three subjects overlap but ask different questions. Economics studies how scarce resources are allocated: what to produce, how, and for whom. Commerce studies the institutions and services that carry out exchange. Industry studies production itself — extraction, manufacturing and construction.

A factory that turns cocoa into chocolate is industry. The bank that finances the cocoa purchase, the ship that carries it and the insurer that covers the cargo are commerce. The economist asks why cocoa prices rose; the commerce student asks which channel moves the beans to the buyer.

This is why 'industry' and 'commerce' are not synonyms in JAMB questions. Industry produces; commerce distributes and supports. A question that names farming, mining or manufacturing is pointing at production, not trade.

Within commerce, trade is narrower than the subject. Trade is the exchange act; commerce includes trade plus aids. A useful test: if the activity earns money by moving, storing, financing, protecting or informing trade, it is an aid; if it earns money by buying and reselling, it is trade.
bullets: Economics explains allocation; commerce explains exchange institutions; industry explains production.
Trade is the exchange act; commerce is trade plus aids to trade.
Farming, mining and manufacturing are production, not aids to trade.

content.heading: Go deeper: The chain from production to consumption
paragraphs: Trace a bag of rice. The farmer produces paddy; a miller processes it; a wholesaler buys in bulk; a retailer breaks the bulk; a transporter moves it; a warehouse stores it; a bank finances each purchase; an insurer covers the stock; an advertiser creates demand. Each link adds utility or lowers the cost of the next link.

Commerce is the coordination of that chain. When one link fails — a bad road, a closed bank, an uninsured fire — the whole chain slows. This is why traders care about infrastructure and credit even though they do not produce the rice.

The chain also explains margins. Each intermediary earns a return for a service: bulk-breaking, storage, transport, risk-bearing or information. A question that asks why prices rise between farm and market is usually asking which link added a cost.
bullets: Each intermediary adds utility or lowers the cost of the next link.
A failure at one link slows the whole chain.
Intermediary margins pay for bulk-breaking, storage, transport, risk and information.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why intermediaries earn a margin
paragraphs: A buyer sometimes asks why a bag of rice costs more in the city than at the farm. Part of the gap is transport, storage and risk. The trader who buys at harvest and sells later is paid for waiting, and for accepting the chance that prices fall before the sale.

Each intermediary also performs a service the next link would otherwise have to do. A wholesaler breaks a lorry-load into smaller lots; a retailer breaks those lots into household sizes; a warehouse keeper keeps stock dry; a bank provides credit so the trader does not need all the cash at once. Remove one link and another party must take on its work, usually at a higher cost.

Margins can still become excessive when a link controls access to a market. That is a competition problem, not proof that intermediaries are useless. For exams, the safe rule is that a margin is earned by a service: bulk-breaking, storage, transport, risk-bearing or information. A trader who adds no service is soon bypassed by buyers and sellers who deal directly.
bullets: A margin pays for a service, not for doing nothing.
Removing a link shifts its work to someone else.
Excess margins point to weak competition.

content.question: A trader buys 200 bags of rice, stores them for two months and insures the warehouse. Identify one trade activity and two aids to trade in the story.
hints: Trade is the buying and selling itself — here, buying the rice to resell.
Storage and insurance support the trade without being the exchange.
A strong answer names the purchase as trade, then warehousing and insurance as aids.

lessons.title: E-commerce and E-business
lessons.objective: Define e-commerce and e-business, distinguish them, and name the B2C, B2B, C2C and B2G forms.

content.heading: E-commerce
paragraphs: E-commerce is buying and selling over electronic networks. E-business is wider: it covers every business process done electronically, from stock control to customer service.

content.heading: A trader moves to WhatsApp
paragraphs: A Lagos cloth seller posts designs on WhatsApp and Instagram. Customers pay by transfer, and a dispatch rider delivers the fabric. She has not opened a shop, but she now sells to buyers in three states.

E-commerce is the buying and selling of goods and services over electronic networks, especially the internet. E-business is wider: it covers every business process done electronically, including stock control, payroll, supplier records and customer service. Every e-commerce transaction is e-business, but not every e-business activity is e-commerce.
bullets: E-commerce = online exchange; e-business = all electronic business processes.
A firm doing its accounts in the cloud is doing e-business, not e-commerce.
content.takeaway: E-commerce is the sale; e-business is the whole electronic operation.

check.question: A firm keeps payroll and supplier records online but sells only in its shop. What is it doing?
check.why: Electronic processes are e-business; an online sale is needed for e-commerce.

visual.caption: E-commerce is the online sale; e-business is every process behind and around it.

rows.right: Was a business process done electronically?

content.heading: Who is selling to whom
paragraphs: E-commerce is classified by who is on each side of the transaction. In business-to-consumer (B2C), a firm sells to households, as Jumia does. In business-to-business (B2B), firms sell to other firms, such as a manufacturer supplying a retailer.

Consumer-to-consumer (C2C) uses a platform to connect two consumers, as when one person sells a phone to another on a marketplace. Business-to-government (B2G) covers firms supplying government agencies. Some writers add government-to-citizen (G2C) for public services online. The labels describe the parties, not the technology or the size of the firm.
bullets: B2C sells to households; B2B sells to firms; C2C connects consumers.
The category depends on who buys and who sells.
content.takeaway: Name the two parties, and the e-commerce type follows.

check.question: A hotel booking site lets individuals book rooms from a hotel company. Which type is that?
check.why: A business is selling to individual consumers, so it is B2C.

content.heading: Cheap to reach, costly to trust
paragraphs: E-commerce lowers the cost of reaching distant buyers and lets a small trader compete without a shop. It also creates new costs. Goods must be delivered, payments must be secured, and buyers must trust that what they ordered will arrive.

In Nigeria, descriptive addresses make delivery depend on phone calls and landmarks. Power and data costs raise the price of running an online store. Fraud and fake products make buyers cautious. Successful platforms answer these problems with ratings, return policies, escrow-style payment holds and clear complaint channels.
bullets: E-commerce cuts distance costs but adds delivery, trust and fraud risks.
Payment, fulfilment, trust and redress are part of the system.
content.takeaway: An online shop is a delivery and trust business as much as a website.

check.question: Which problem is created by e-commerce rather than solved by it?
options: Buyers can order from another city.
A small trader can reach more customers.
Buyers must trust a seller they cannot meet.
Prices can be compared without travelling.
check.why: Distance selling removes the face-to-face check, so trust becomes a new cost.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Every e-commerce transaction is e-business, but e-business is not always e-commerce. Look for an online sale before choosing e-commerce.

content.problem: A firm advertises on its website but accepts orders only by phone and cash. Is it doing e-commerce? A. Yes, because it has a website B. Yes, because advertising is electronic C. No, because no sale is completed online D. No, because it has no app

steps.reason: It requires buying or selling over an electronic network.
steps.result: A website alone is not enough.

steps.reason: Orders are placed by phone and paid in cash.
Electronic advertising is e-business, not e-commerce.

content.heading: Go deeper: What makes e-commerce work in Nigeria
paragraphs: An online sale needs four things beyond a website: a payment route, a delivery route, trust, and a way to reverse failure. Nigeria's payment route matured with bank transfers, cards and mobile money; logistics firms now cover many cities; and marketplaces use ratings, escrow-style holds and return policies to build trust.

Each layer carries a local constraint. Addresses are often descriptive rather than postal, so delivery depends on phone calls and landmarks. Power and data costs raise the price of running a store. Fraud and fake products make buyers cautious, which raises the cost of convincing them.

Regulation matters too. Consumer protection, data protection and payment rules determine what a platform must disclose and how it must handle complaints. A business that ignores them faces chargebacks, sanctions and reputational loss.

The exam link is direct: e-commerce is not just 'selling on the internet'. It is the whole chain of payment, fulfilment, trust and redress. That is why a question about the main challenge of e-commerce in Nigeria may point to logistics or trust rather than to website design.
bullets: E-commerce needs payment, fulfilment, trust and redress, not just a website.
Nigerian constraints include descriptive addresses, power costs, data costs and fraud.
Consumer and data-protection rules shape what platforms must disclose.

content.heading: Go deeper: Trust, payment and redress
paragraphs: An online buyer often pays before holding the goods, so every e-commerce system must answer three questions: will the goods arrive, will they be as described, and what happens if they are not?

Payment protection is the first answer. Card chargebacks, escrow accounts and platform-held funds let a buyer recover money when a seller fails to deliver. The platform becomes a trusted middleman, which is why a marketplace can charge a fee that a simple website cannot.

Redress is the second. Return windows, dispute desks and published seller ratings give the buyer a route after a failure. Consumer-protection law may add a right to a refund or replacement, but the practical route is usually the platform's complaint process.

The third is information. Clear photographs, sizes, delivery times and seller history reduce the gap between what the buyer expects and what arrives. Exam questions about e-commerce challenges often point to trust and logistics rather than to web design. A seller who accepts cash on delivery reverses the risk, but may lose buyers who refuse to pay. That is why reviews and return policies are business infrastructure, not decoration.
bullets: Buyers pay before delivery, so trust must be designed into the system.
Escrow and chargebacks protect payment; returns and ratings protect quality.
Consumer law sets a floor; platform rules do the daily work.

content.heading: Go deeper: What e-business adds inside the firm
paragraphs: E-business is not just a shopfront. Inside a firm, it covers stock records, payroll, supplier orders, customer databases and internal reporting. A supermarket that tracks every sale by barcode is doing e-business even if customers pay cash at a till.

The gain is information. Electronic records let a manager see which goods sell, reorder before stock runs out and compare suppliers. The cost is dependence: a firm that cannot access its systems may struggle to trade, and data breaches become a business risk. The same systems also create audit trails that help a firm detect theft and waste.

For exams, keep the boundary clear. E-business is the wider category of electronic processes; e-commerce is the subset that buys or sells. A question that mentions online payment or an online order is about e-commerce.
bullets: E-business includes internal processes that never face a customer.
Electronic records improve control but create dependence and data risk.
E-commerce is the buying-and-selling subset of e-business.

content.question: A book seller takes orders on Instagram and payment by bank transfer. Name the e-commerce type and one trust problem she must solve.
hints: The seller is a business and the buyers are individual readers.
Trust problems include fake payment alerts, non-delivery and goods that differ from the photograph.

lessons.title: What an Occupation Is
lessons.objective: Define occupation, distinguish it from employment, and name the three groups of work.

content.heading: Occupation
paragraphs: An occupation is the regular work a person does for a living. It is wider than a job: a teacher who changes schools still has the same occupation.

content.heading: The teacher who changed schools
paragraphs: A teacher leaves a private school for a public one. Her salary, employer and timetable change. Her occupation does not: she is still a teacher, because the kind of work is the same.

An occupation is the regular work through which a person earns a living. Employment is the contract under which that work is done; occupation is the kind of work itself. A self-employed tailor has an occupation but no employer. An unemployed nurse still has an occupation, because the work type has not disappeared.
bullets: Occupation = work type; employment = the contract to do it.
A person can change jobs without changing occupation.
content.takeaway: Occupation names the work; employment names who pays for it.

check.question: A nurse resigns and is looking for work. What is true?
options: She has an occupation but no employment.
She has employment but no occupation.
She has neither an occupation nor employment.
check.why: The work type remains; only the contract has ended.

visual.caption: A change of employer changes the employment, not the occupation.

rows.right: The paid contract to do it
Her post at one private school

rows.left: Would it survive a change of employer?
rows.right: Does it end with the contract?

content.heading: Three families of work
paragraphs: The syllabus groups occupations by what they do. Industrial occupations produce physical goods: farming, mining, manufacturing and construction. Commercial occupations make exchange possible: traders, bankers, insurers, transporters and advertisers.

Service occupations provide direct help, skill or expertise: teaching, medicine, law, accounting, the civil service and entertainment. The output is not a physical good; it is an improvement in the customer's condition or capability. The three groups are not ranked: a country needs all of them, and many workers move between them.
bullets: Industrial produces goods, commercial supports exchange, services serve people directly.
A banker is commercial; a teacher is service.
A person may work in more than one group over a career.
content.takeaway: Ask what the work produces: a good, an exchange, or a direct service.

check.question: A dispatch rider carries goods for an online store. Which group is the work in?
check.why: Transport is an aid to trade, so the occupation is commercial.

content.heading: Why work matters beyond the wage
paragraphs: Occupations produce the goods and services people use, create income for households and generate tax revenue for government. They also give people identity, structure and a way to use their talents. Work also transmits skills: experienced workers train the next generation on the job.

A country with diverse occupations is less exposed to a single shock. When one sector fails, workers with transferable skills can move, and the economy keeps producing. An economy that depends on one export is vulnerable to a fall in its price.
bullets: Occupations create income, output and tax revenue.
Diversity reduces dependence on one sector.
Work passes skills from one generation to the next.
content.takeaway: Work is both a livelihood and a source of national resilience.

check.question: Why does a country with many occupations suffer less when one sector fails?
options: Workers can move to other sectors.
Its government spends less on schools.
check.why: Transferable skills let workers move, so output does not collapse with one sector.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A transporter has a commercial occupation because transport supports trade; the trade itself is the buying and selling. Do not call every worker a trader.

content.problem: A woman buys tomatoes from farmers and resells them in the city. Which type of occupation is she in? A. Extractive B. Manufacturing C. Commercial D. Service

steps.reason: She buys in order to resell, which is trade.
steps.predictPrompt: Does she grow or process the tomatoes herself?

steps.reason: Extractive and manufacturing occupations create or process goods; she does neither.
A service is rendered directly to a client; she sells goods to buyers.

content.heading: Go deeper: Occupation, employment, career and profession
paragraphs: Four terms are often confused. An occupation is the kind of work; employment is the contract under which it is done; a career is the sequence of jobs and roles a person holds over time; a profession is an occupation that requires specialised training, a licence and a code of conduct.

The distinctions explain odd-sounding facts. A self-employed tailor has an occupation but no employer. An unemployed nurse still has an occupation, because the work type has not disappeared. A lawyer who moves from private practice to government has changed employment and maybe her career path, but not her profession.

Professions are regulated because their work carries risk or trust: medicine, law, accounting and engineering. Entry requires recognised training, and misconduct can lead to loss of the licence. A trade such as carpentry can be skilled without being a profession in this strict sense.
For exams, remember the test: occupation names the work, employment names the contract, career names the progression, and profession names the licensed specialism.
bullets: Occupation = work type; employment = contract; career = sequence; profession = licensed specialism.
A self-employed person has an occupation but no employer.
Unemployment removes the job, not the occupation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Specialisation and the labour market
paragraphs: Occupations multiply because of division of labour. When work is split into tasks, each task can be done by someone who does it often and well. Specialisation raises output, but it also makes workers dependent on exchange: the tailor needs the farmer, and the farmer needs the tailor.

The labour market matches people to work. Employers hire by skill and experience; workers invest in training to raise their value; wages move with demand and supply. A shortage of engineers raises their pay, while a surplus of a narrow skill lowers it.

Two kinds of skill matter differently. Specific skills are useful in one firm or industry; transferable skills move across employers. Automation and new technology shift demand toward transferable and technical skills, which is why training policy focuses on adaptability rather than a single job.

In Nigeria, apprenticeships and informal training carry much of the skill formation that formal institutions do not reach. That makes the quality of training uneven, but it also keeps practical trades alive.
bullets: Specialisation raises output and creates dependence on exchange.
Wages respond to the demand for and supply of each skill.
Transferable skills protect workers when technology or demand shifts.

content.heading: Go deeper: The informal sector in Nigeria
paragraphs: A large share of Nigerian work is informal: street trading, repairs, transport, artisanal production and personal services. Informal work is not the same as illegal work. It is work that is not registered, regulated or recorded in the same way as formal employment.

Its advantages are easy entry, low starting capital and flexibility. A trader can start with small capital, set her own hours and keep the income close to the household. It absorbs workers when formal jobs are scarce.

Its disadvantages are protection and finance. Informal workers usually lack pensions, health insurance and written contracts, and lenders cannot easily assess their income. Because records are thin, the tax base is narrow too.

Policy therefore faces a trade-off. Registering and taxing the informal sector can widen revenue, but heavy-handed collection can push fragile businesses out of operation. The usual prescription is to lower the cost of formalising and to pair registration with access to credit and social protection.
bullets: Informal work is unregistered, not necessarily illegal.
It offers easy entry and flexibility but weak protection and credit access.
Formalisation works best when paired with credit and social protection.

content.question: Classify each occupation and give one reason: (a) a fisherman, (b) an insurance broker, (c) a secondary-school teacher.
hints: Ask whether the work extracts, supports exchange, or serves a person directly.
The fisherman extracts from nature; the broker supports trade; the teacher renders a service.

lessons.title: Industrial Occupations
lessons.objective: Classify industrial work as extractive, manufacturing or construction, and explain how the three stages depend on each other.

content.heading: Industrial occupations
paragraphs: Industrial occupations create physical goods. They are grouped into extractive, manufacturing and construction work, and each stage feeds the next.

content.heading: From quarry to road
paragraphs: A quarry blasts limestone from a hillside. A cement factory grinds it into cement. A construction firm mixes the cement and pours a road. Three different occupations, one chain of production.

Extractive occupations take raw materials directly from nature: farming, fishing, mining, quarrying and forestry. They are the first stage of production. Without them, factories would have nothing to process and builders would have nothing to build with. A fisherman and a farmer are extractive even when they use modern equipment. The stage is named for what it takes, not for how large the business is.
bullets: Extractive work takes raw materials from nature.
Farming, fishing, mining, quarrying and forestry are extractive.
Extraction supplies the raw materials for every other stage.
content.takeaway: Extraction begins the production chain by taking from nature.

check.question: Which of these is an extractive occupation?
check.why: A quarry takes stone from the ground; the mill and builder process or use it.

visual.caption: Each industrial stage hands its output to the next, from nature to a fixed asset.

content.heading: Making and building
paragraphs: Manufacturing turns raw materials into finished or intermediate goods. A flour mill turns wheat into flour; a textile mill turns cotton into cloth; a cement plant turns limestone into cement. The output is a new good with a new use.

Construction builds fixed assets: houses, roads, bridges, schools and factories. It uses manufactured materials but does not mass-produce them. A building stays where it is built, so construction work is tied to a site. A house and a road are both construction, because both are fixed in place.
bullets: Manufacturing transforms raw materials into goods.
Construction builds fixed assets on site.
Construction output cannot be moved to another place.
content.takeaway: Manufacturing changes the material; construction puts it in place.

check.question: A firm turns cassava into garri. Which industrial stage is that?
check.why: The cassava is processed into a new good, which is manufacturing.

content.heading: Why the stages depend on each other
paragraphs: The three stages are linked. A poor harvest raises the price of flour. A cement shortage delays road building. A construction boom raises demand for cement, steel and timber, which in turn raises demand for quarrying and manufacturing. A fall in construction can therefore reach back to the quarry and the factory.

Industrial occupations also create jobs outside the factory. Transport firms move the raw materials, banks finance the equipment, and insurers cover the plant. This is why an industrial policy that supports one stage usually affects the others.
bullets: A shortage at one stage raises costs at the next.
Industrial work pulls in transport, finance and insurance.
Demand travels down the chain as well as up.
content.takeaway: Industrial stages rise and fall together.

check.question: A building boom is most likely to increase demand for which occupation first?
check.why: Construction needs stone, cement and steel, so extraction and manufacturing rise first.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Extractive does not mean 'simple'. Farming and mining are extractive because they take from nature, however much machinery they use.

content.problem: A firm buys cassava from farmers and turns it into garri. Which type of occupation is the firm in? A. Extractive B. Manufacturing C. Construction D. Commercial

steps.reason: The firm changes cassava into a different product, garri.
steps.result: Processing raw material into a good is manufacturing.
steps.predictPrompt: Does the firm take the cassava from the ground itself?

steps.reason: The farmers extract the cassava; the firm buys it.
The firm neither builds a fixed asset nor merely resells the cassava.

content.question: Classify each occupation and name its industrial stage: (a) a fisherman, (b) a cement factory, (c) a road builder.
hints: Ask whether the work takes from nature, changes a material, or builds on a site.
The fisherman is extractive; the factory is manufacturing; the road builder is construction.

lessons.title: Commercial and Service Occupations
lessons.objective: Distinguish commercial occupations from service occupations, and explain why a service is not an aid to trade.

content.heading: Commercial and service work
paragraphs: Commercial occupations support trade; service occupations serve people directly. Both sell something, but only commercial work is an aid to trade.

content.heading: The banker and the teacher
paragraphs: A banker approves a loan so a trader can buy stock. A teacher prepares a pupil for an exam. Both are paid for their work, but the banker's work exists to make a sale happen, while the teacher's work exists to improve the pupil.

Commercial occupations make exchange possible. They include traders — wholesalers and retailers — and the aids to trade: bankers, insurers, transporters, warehouse keepers, advertisers and communication workers. A banker does not sell the goods, but without the bank the sale may not happen. The bank earns a fee or interest, not a share of the trader's profit.
bullets: Commercial = trade plus aids to trade.
A banker is commercial because banking supports exchange.
content.takeaway: Commercial work exists to move or support a sale.

check.question: Which occupation is commercial?
check.why: Warehousing is an aid to trade; the others provide direct services.

content.heading: Work that serves the person
paragraphs: Service occupations provide direct help, skill or expertise. Teaching, medicine, law, accounting, the civil service, catering and entertainment are services. The output is not a physical good; it is an improvement in the customer's condition or capability. A service cannot be stored for later: it is produced and consumed at once.

Some service workers also support business — a lawyer may draft a supply contract — but the service itself is the product. The client buys the lawyer's time and judgement, not a share of the goods being sold.
bullets: Services are rendered directly to a person or client.
A service is not an aid to trade just because a business buys it.
content.takeaway: Service work sells help or expertise, not the movement of goods.

check.question: A lawyer drafts a contract for a trading company. Why is the lawyer's occupation still a service?
options: The lawyer owns the goods being sold.
The lawyer sells time and judgement directly to the client.
check.why: The client buys the lawyer's expertise; supporting a trader does not make the work an aid to trade.

content.heading: Telling them apart under exam pressure
paragraphs: The exam distinction is purpose. Commercial work exists to support trade; service work exists to serve the person who needs it. Transport is commercial because it moves goods for sale. A bus carrying passengers is a service, even though both use the same road.

When an option is ambiguous, ask who the customer is and what they buy. If the customer is buying help with their own condition, the work is a service. If the customer is buying a step in the movement or financing of goods, the work is commercial.
bullets: A goods transporter is commercial; a passenger bus is a service.
Ask what the customer is buying.
content.takeaway: Purpose decides the group, not the vehicle or the job title.

check.question: A taxi carries a trader to a market. Is the taxi service commercial or service?
options: Commercial, because the passenger is a trader
Commercial, because the taxi uses a road
Service, because it carries a person rather than goods for sale
Industrial, because it uses a vehicle
check.why: The customer buys personal transport; moving goods for trade would make it commercial.

visual.caption: The two groups are separated by purpose, not by job title or workplace.

rows.left: A step in moving or financing goods
rows.right: Help with their own condition or task

rows.left: A trading margin, fee or interest
rows.right: A salary or a fee for expertise

rows.left: Does it move or finance goods for sale?
rows.right: Does it serve the person directly?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A transporter has a commercial occupation because transport supports trade; the trade itself is the buying and selling. Do not call every worker a trader.

content.problem: A woman buys tomatoes from farmers and resells them in the city. Which type of occupation is she in? A. Extractive B. Manufacturing C. Commercial D. Service

steps.reason: She buys in order to resell, which is trade.
steps.predictPrompt: Does she grow or process the tomatoes herself?

steps.reason: Extractive and manufacturing occupations create or process goods; she does neither.
A service is rendered directly to a client; she sells goods to buyers.

content.question: Classify each occupation and give one reason: (a) a wholesaler, (b) a warehouse keeper, (c) a doctor.
hints: Ask whether the work buys and sells, supports a sale, or serves a person directly.
The wholesaler trades; the warehouse keeper supports trade; the doctor serves the patient.

lessons.title: Choosing an Occupation
lessons.objective: Name the factors that shape occupational choice and explain how skill, interest, demand and capital interact.

content.heading: Choosing an occupation
paragraphs: Occupational choice is shaped by skill, interest, income, demand, capital and location. Good choices align ability, interest and opportunity.

content.heading: The job that looked perfect
paragraphs: A student loves drawing and wins a place to study architecture. Two years later she discovers that the course requires mathematics she avoided, and that jobs in her city are few. Interest was necessary, but it was not enough. Interest is a starting point, not a plan. She should have checked the course requirements and the local job market before choosing.

Choice is shaped by qualifications and skills, interest and aptitude, expected income, the demand for workers, the capital needed, location, family influence and government policy. Health and age also limit some options.
bullets: Skills and qualifications decide what is possible.
Interest and aptitude decide what is sustainable.
content.takeaway: A choice that ignores ability or demand will not last.

check.question: A student loves music but has no training and no money for a conservatory. Which two factors limit her most directly?
check.why: She lacks the training (skill) and the funds (capital); interest is present, not limiting.

content.heading: The factors interact
paragraphs: In practice the factors interact. A high salary cannot compensate for a job a person cannot do or does not want. A strong interest cannot create demand where no jobs exist. Capital matters more in some trades than others: a tailor can start small, while a factory needs machinery.

Location matters because work is local for most people. Family can open a door or narrow a choice. Government policy shifts demand through scholarships, licensing and public employment. A good decision weighs several factors together rather than chasing one.
bullets: Demand, capital and location decide what is available.
Family, health and government policy also shape choice.
content.takeaway: Balance what you can do, what you want and what the market needs.

check.question: A town has many trained teachers but only one school. Which factor most limits the teachers' choice?
check.why: The number of jobs is the demand for teachers; training is already complete.

content.heading: Skills that travel
paragraphs: The labour market matches people to work. Employers hire by skill and experience; workers invest in training to raise their value; wages move with demand and supply. A shortage of engineers raises their pay, while a surplus of a narrow skill lowers it.

Two kinds of skill matter differently. Specific skills are useful in one firm or industry; transferable skills move across employers. Automation and new technology shift demand toward transferable and technical skills, so training that teaches adaptability protects a worker better than training for one job. A worker who can learn new tools is less exposed to automation.
bullets: Wages respond to the demand for and supply of each skill.
Transferable skills protect workers when demand shifts.
content.takeaway: Choose work that builds skills you can carry elsewhere.

check.question: Which skill is most transferable?
options: Using a single company's login system
check.why: Clear writing is useful across employers; the others are specific to one workplace.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In questions about choice, distinguish what the worker can do (skill), what they want (interest) and what exists (demand). The factor named in the stem is the answer.

content.problem: A student chooses teaching because a scholarship pays for training and schools in her town are hiring. Which two factors are at work? A. Interest and age B. Government policy and demand C. Capital and family D. Health and location

steps.reason: A scholarship is a government or institutional policy that lowers the cost of training.
steps.predictPrompt: What is happening to teaching jobs in her town?

steps.reason: Schools are hiring, so there is demand for teachers.
Only option B names government policy and demand.

content.question: A woman wants to open a bakery. Name three factors she should weigh and say why each matters.
hints: Consider what she can do, what she can afford, and who will buy.
Skills affect quality; capital buys equipment; demand and location decide whether the bread sells.

lessons.title: Production
lessons.objective: Identify the factors of production and their rewards, distinguish division of labour from specialisation, classify types of production, and state the relationship between production, specialisation and exchange.

content.heading: Production
paragraphs: A cassava farmer, a miller and a trader each do one part of the work. Production combines land, labour, capital and enterprise to make goods useful, and specialisation links that effort to exchange.

content.heading: The four factors and what each earns
paragraphs: A cassava farm in Oyo State uses a plot, family labour, a grinding machine and the owner who organises the work. Those four resources are the factors of production, and each earns a reward for its contribution. Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and the entrepreneur earns profit.

Land is fixed and varies in quality, so it cannot be moved to where it is most needed. Labour is perishable, because an unused day of work cannot be stored, while capital wears out and needs replacement. The entrepreneur is distinct because he bears uncertainty and combines the other three.
bullets: Land and natural resources earn rent for their use.
Labour earns wages, and its supply depends on skills and population.
Capital earns interest, while entrepreneurship earns profit as a reward for risk.
content.takeaway: Every good combines land, labour, capital and enterprise, each earning a distinct reward.

check.question: A farmer pays rent for a plot, wages for workers and interest to a bank. What is the farmer, as organiser, earning from risk?
check.why: The entrepreneur organises the factors and earns profit for bearing risk.

content.heading: Division of labour and specialisation
paragraphs: When a household makes everything it needs, output is low and time is wasted. Division of labour splits work into narrow tasks, while specialisation means concentrating on the task a person does best. A market in Onitsha makes the point clear, with a carpenter, a tailor and a trader each doing one main job.

The two are confused in examinations, so keep the line sharp. Division of labour describes splitting work into tasks; specialisation describes a worker concentrating on one task. Specialisation raises skill, speed and output, but it also creates dependence, because each specialist needs others for what he no longer makes.
bullets: Division of labour splits a job into stages, such as carpentry into cutting, shaping and joining.
Specialisation builds dexterity and saves time, so output rises per worker.
Specialisation limits variety and makes the worker depend on exchange for other goods.
content.takeaway: Division splits the work; specialisation concentrates the worker on one task.

check.question: A tailor now sews only seams while others cut and press. What has happened?
check.why: Work is split into tasks and the tailor concentrates on one task.

content.heading: Types of production and the link to exchange
paragraphs: Primary production takes goods directly from nature, such as farming, fishing, mining and quarrying. Secondary production transforms those materials, such as milling cassava into garri or weaving cotton into cloth. Tertiary production provides services, including teaching, banking, transport and healthcare, which improve the user rather than create a physical good.

Production, specialisation and exchange form one chain. A farmer who specialises in yam produces more than he uses, so he exchanges the surplus for tools, food and services. Exchange therefore completes specialisation, while without it the gains from specialisation would remain unused.
bullets: Primary extracts from nature; secondary transforms materials; tertiary renders services.
Cassava milling is secondary, while banking and teaching are tertiary services.
Specialisation creates a surplus, and exchange lets the producer obtain what he does not make.
content.takeaway: Nature, transformation and services are distinct stages that depend on exchange.

check.question: Milling cassava into garri is which type of production?
check.why: The raw material is transformed into a new good, which is secondary production.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In an examination, match each factor to its reward before deciding. Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and enterprise earns profit. If the option swaps a reward, reject it at once.

content.problem: A yam farmer hires labour, rents a tractor and borrows tools. Which reward does the tractor owner earn? A. Rent B. Wages C. Interest D. Profit

steps.reason: A tractor is capital, meaning equipment provided for production.
steps.result: Capital earns interest for its use.

steps.reason: Rent pays for land, while wages pay for labour.
Capital supplied for a payment receives interest as its return.

content.question: Classify each activity as primary, secondary or tertiary production: (a) fishing in Lake Chad, (b) weaving cotton into cloth, (c) teaching in a secondary school.
hints: Ask whether the work takes from nature, transforms a material, or renders a service.
Fishing extracts from nature, so it is primary production.
Weaving transforms cotton and teaching serves learners, so they are secondary and tertiary.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why each factor behaves differently
paragraphs: Land is often described as free from nature, but in Nigeria its use is governed by family, community and state arrangements. A plot cannot be moved, so a good location keeps its value while a remote plot may remain underused even when labour is cheap. Fertility also varies, which is why the same labour produces different harvests on different soils.

Labour cannot be stored, so a day lost to illness or idle waiting is lost for good. Wages must therefore clear the market for effort today, while skills determine how much one hour can produce. Capital behaves differently again, because machines depreciate, need maintenance and must be replaced before they trap the firm in high repair costs.

The entrepreneur is the only factor paid from what remains after the other factors are settled. That residual is profit, and it may be large when the venture succeeds and negative when it fails. This is why entrepreneurship is linked to risk rather than to effort alone; the organiser can work hard yet earn nothing if the market turns against the product.
bullets: Land is immobile and heterogeneous, so location and quality shape output.
Labour is perishable and skill-sensitive, so incentives and training matter.
Capital depreciates and needs funds, while enterprise bears residual risk.

content.heading: Go deeper: Gains and limits of dividing work
paragraphs: Division of labour raises output because repetition builds speed, precision and familiarity with tools. A carpenter who only cuts, shapes and joins all day learns faster than a generalist who switches tasks hourly. The market therefore rewards those who master a narrow operation, especially where equipment and training improve with use.

Time is saved when workers stop moving between tasks and when learning is not repeated. A tailor in Kano who only sews seams can finish far more garments than one who must measure, cut, sew, press and sell. Machines deepen the gain, because a single operation can be mechanised more easily than a whole craft.

The limits matter for examinations and for real markets. Very narrow work can become monotonous, skill can become obsolete when methods change, and a specialist depends on others for food, money and tools. If transport or communication fails, the specialist cannot easily fall back on self-sufficiency, so the gain depends on reliable exchange.
bullets: Repetition builds skill and speed, while staying on one task saves time and training.
Machines gain most when a single operation is repeated at scale.
Specialists gain output but lose self-sufficiency and bear dependence risk.

content.heading: Go deeper: How surplus becomes trade
paragraphs: Specialisation means each producer makes more of one item than the household can consume. That surplus is the source of trade, because it gives the producer something to offer in return. A rice farmer in Ebonyi State who specialises in rice must exchange part of the harvest for palm oil, tools, schooling and healthcare.

Exchange also reveals what the market values. If buyers will exchange more food for a load of rice than for a load of another crop, its relative reward has risen. Prices therefore steer specialisation, encouraging producers to concentrate where the return is highest, though the signal may mislead when demand changes quickly.

The chain can also run backwards. When exchange breaks down through poor roads, insecurity or lack of money, producers reduce specialisation and return to mixed farming. Output falls not because skills have vanished, but because the surplus cannot reach buyers. For JAMB answers, state the sequence clearly: production creates goods, specialisation creates surplus, and exchange distributes it.
bullets: Surplus from specialisation must be exchanged, or the gain is wasted.
Relative prices steer what producers specialise in, but signals can lag.
Failure of transport or money can reverse specialisation into self-sufficiency.

lessons.title: Money
lessons.objective: Discuss the origin of money, analyse the forms and qualities of money, and appraise the functions of money.

content.heading: Money
paragraphs: A tomato seller at Mile 12 market will not swap tomatoes for a haircut she does not need. Money solves that problem by acting as a generally accepted medium through which every trader can exchange.

content.heading: From barter to a generally accepted medium
paragraphs: Under barter, goods are exchanged directly for other goods. A farmer with yam must find a butcher who wants exactly that yam and can offer meat in return. That need to find a matching want is called the double coincidence of wants, and it makes every exchange slow and uncertain.

Barter also forces awkward burdens. Goods may be bulky, perish bread or foul water, split badly or rot before a buyer appears. Money emerged as an item everyone would accept in settlement, so each seller could take money and later buy what was needed, and once acceptance spread it began to circulate.
bullets: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants, which is rare in large markets.
Bulky, perishable or indivisible goods make direct exchange costly and risky.
Money emerges when general acceptance removes the need for a matching want.
content.takeaway: Barter fails on matching wants; money succeeds through general acceptance.

check.question: A yam farmer cannot find a buyer who wants his yam at that moment. Which barter problem is this?
check.why: Barter needs two matching wants at one time, which is rare in large markets.

content.heading: Forms of money and the qualities they need
paragraphs: Commodity money has value in its own substance, such as cowries, salt or gold used in exchange. Fiat money is given value by law and general acceptance rather than by its material, as with paper notes and coins issued by the state. Bank money consists of deposits and transfers recorded by banks, which now carry much daily trade.

Good money must show several qualities. It should be accepted everywhere, hard to counterfeit and durable enough to survive handling. It should be portable in large value, divisible into small change, uniform in value and stable so that its purchasing power does not swing wildly.
bullets: Commodity money rests on substance; fiat rests on law and acceptance; bank money is transferable deposits.
Acceptance, durability, portability and divisibility let money circulate in many payments.
Stability means the value of money does not change too fast.
content.takeaway: Acceptance, durability, portability, divisibility and stability make money usable.

check.question: Notes and coins issued by the state and accepted by law are which form of money?
check.why: Fiat money has value by law and acceptance, not by its material substance.

content.heading: What money does in the market
paragraphs: Money first serves as a medium of exchange, breaking the need for a matching want. A trader sells tomatoes for naira and later buys rice with the same naira. Because everyone accepts it, money links distant sellers and shortens the time goods spend waiting for a buyer.

Money also measures value, so that different goods can be priced and compared. It acts as a store of value, allowing purchasing power to be kept for later use, and as a standard of deferred payments, so debts and instalments can be fixed in money terms. A shopkeeper who keeps stock value in money avoids holding perishable goods as savings.
bullets: As a medium of exchange, money removes the double coincidence of wants.
As a measure and store, money lets prices be compared and value be saved.
As a standard of deferred payments, money fixes debts for future settlement.
content.takeaway: Money exchanges, measures, stores and settles future payments in one unit.

check.question: A retailer buys stock now and pays the wholesaler next month in a fixed naira sum. Which function is used?
check.why: The debt is fixed in money for settlement at a later date.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A medium of exchange and a measure of value are different. Medium settles today's purchase, while measure prices goods for comparison. If the choice speaks of comparing or pricing, it is measuring, not exchanging.

content.problem: Which of these is a quality of good money? A. Perishability B. Divisibility C. Limited acceptance D. Instability of value

steps.reason: Good money must be acceptable, durable, portable and divisible.
Perishability, limited acceptance and instability weaken circulation.
steps.result: A, C and D are defects, not qualities.

steps.reason: Divisibility allows small change from one unit of money.

content.question: A trader accepts naira for goods today but keeps money for school fees next term. Name the two functions shown and explain why they are different.
hints: The first use settles today's sale, so it is the medium of exchange.
The second use keeps purchasing power for later, so it is the store of value.
One moves value now, while the other holds value until it is needed.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why direct exchange breaks down
paragraphs: Barter needs two wants to meet at once. The yam farmer needs meat, and the butcher needs yam, in the right quantities and at the same moment. In a village that meeting may occur, but in a city market with thousands of goods the chance of pairing every want at once falls sharply.

The failure is economic and practical. Indirect trade through an intermediate good does not solve the problem if that good is itself perishable, indivisible or hard to value. A bag of rice split for a small purchase loses value, while a live goat cannot be divided without destroying its worth. Transport also matters, because bulky goods cannot easily reach a matching buyer.

Money solves the meeting problem by inserting a token that everyone accepts. The seller no longer needs to find the final consumer of his good; he only needs to find a buyer of money, which is everyone. That single change widens markets and lets producers specialise, because the buyer for their surplus is no longer a single household but the whole market.
bullets: The double coincidence fails when thousands of wants must pair at once.
Perishability and indivisibility make barter costly even when a match is found.
General acceptance widens the market because every seller can accept money.

content.heading: Go deeper: Fiat money, trust and stability
paragraphs: Paper notes and coins have little intrinsic value, so their acceptance depends on trust in the issuer and in other users. Legal tender rules help, because courts and agencies must accept naira for taxes and official payments. Confidence is tested when prices rise quickly, since people then doubt whether money will still buy the same basket next month.

Stability is therefore a quality of money itself, not a wish. When money loses value fast, sellers raise prices to protect themselves, savers avoid holding it, and contracts shorten. Bank money is not exempt, because deposits are only as safe as the bank and the payment system that settles them when the saver wants cash.

Modern payments add another layer. Transfers, cards and mobile payments move bank money without notes changing hands, so portability is high even though nothing physical moves. The risk shifts to the records, the network and the balance behind them. Examinations therefore separate the form, which may be paper, coin or electronic, from the qualities the form must still satisfy.
bullets: Fiat money depends on issuer trust and legal acceptance, not on material value.
Instability shortens contracts and discourages saving, even for bank deposits.
Electronic bank money is portable, but its safety rests on records and networks.

content.heading: Go deeper: Money at work in daily trade
paragraphs: In a Lagos market a single naira note may pass through a tomato seller, a pepper seller and a transport operator before resting in a till. Each time it settles a sale without any of them needing the other's goods. That circulation is the medium of exchange at its simplest, repeated many times a day.

The measure function appears on price tags. A buyer compares a 500 naira measure of tomatoes with a 1500 naira bottle of oil because both are expressed in one unit. The store function appears when a trader banks sales for school fees or rent, keeping value in a form that does not rot. Neither function needs the money to be a good itself.

Deferred payments turn the same unit into a promise. A wholesaler who supplies a retailer on credit fixes the debt in naira, so both parties know what must be paid later. That standard makes instalments, loans and rents workable over time. If the value of money changes sharply, however, the fixed sum buys less or more, so the promise carries risk.
bullets: Circulation in the market shows the medium of exchange in daily use.
Pricing compares goods, while banking keeps value from rotting like food.
Credit fixes a future debt in money, linking present trade to later payment.

lessons.title: Business Units
lessons.objective: Identify the forms and features of business units, analyse registration procedures, examine choice factors, differentiate dissolution from liquidation, state merits and demerits, and state reasons for government ownership of public enterprises.

content.heading: Business Units
paragraphs: A sole trader in Balogun Market, a partnership of tailors and a public corporation form different kinds of business units. The form chosen shapes ownership, liability, capital and how the unit ends.

content.heading: Sole traders to public corporations
paragraphs: A sole proprietorship is owned by one person, who supplies capital and takes all profit and loss. A partnership is owned by two to twenty people under a partnership agreement, sharing capital and profit. A limited liability company is a separate legal person, owned by shareholders whose liability is limited to their shares.

Features differ across the market, with sole traders cheap to start but carrying unlimited liability and limited capital. Partnerships pool skill and capital but can end when a partner dies or leaves. Public corporations are created by law for public service, while cooperative societies are owned by members for mutual benefit.
bullets: Sole proprietorship: one owner, unlimited liability, easy entry and small capital.
Partnership: shared ownership, agreement, pooled capital and shared risk.
Limited company: separate legal person with limited liability for shareholders.
Public corporation and cooperative: created for public service or member benefit.
content.takeaway: Ownership, liability and purpose separate the five common business forms.

check.question: Which business form has unlimited liability and is owned by one person?
check.why: A sole trader owns the business alone and bears unlimited liability.

content.heading: Registration, choice, dissolution and liquidation
paragraphs: A sole trader needs little formal registration, but a partnership should put its terms in writing. A limited company must be registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission, which confirms the name, objects and capital. Registration gives legal identity and lets the company own property, sue and be sued.

Choice therefore depends on capital needs, liability the owner can bear, continuity and control. Dissolution ends the business relationship, such as when partners agree to separate, while liquidation is the formal winding up of a company and sale of its assets to pay debts. Dissolution may simply close the arrangement; liquidation is a legal process.
bullets: Registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission creates a separate legal person for companies.
Dissolution ends the trading relationship; liquidation winds up a company legally.
Small scale and tolerance for risk favour sole trading; large capital favours a company.
content.takeaway: Registration creates the company, and liquidation is its formal legal closure.

check.question: Partners agree to separate and settle accounts among themselves. What is this called?
check.why: Dissolution ends the partnership relationship, while liquidation winds up a company legally.

content.heading: Merits, limits and why government owns enterprises
paragraphs: Sole traders offer quick decisions, low cost and full control, but they lack capital, skills and cover when the owner is absent. Partnerships add skill and pooled funds, yet disputes and unlimited liability remain. Limited companies raise large capital and survive their owners, but registration, audit and reporting cost time and money.

Government owns public enterprises because some services must reach everyone at affordable prices. The National Electric Power Authority and its successors, now under the PHCN heritage, were kept in public hands to supply power as a public service rather than for private profit alone. Water, transport and control of natural resources also motivate ownership, alongside employment and development goals.
bullets: Merits of small forms are low cost and control; their limit is capital and liability.
Companies gain finance and continuity but carry compliance costs.
Public ownership secures universal service, resource control and development, not profit alone.
content.takeaway: Small forms trade control for scale; public ownership trades profit for service.

check.question: Why did government keep electricity in public hands under the PHCN heritage?
options: To supply power as a public service
To favour one trader at Balogun Market
To avoid providing electricity at all
check.why: Public ownership aimed to make power accessible as a service, not for profit alone.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the question asks about liability, choose the limited company. If it asks about cheap entry and one owner, choose the sole proprietorship. Dissolution is not liquidation; liquidation is the formal winding up of a company.

content.problem: A business wants limited liability and separate legal status. Which form should it adopt? A. Sole proprietorship B. Partnership C. Limited liability company D. Cooperative society

steps.reason: Limited liability and separate legal status point to a company.
steps.result: Sole and partnership forms lack that shield.

steps.reason: A company gains legal personality through Corporate Affairs Commission registration.
steps.result: It can own property and be sued separately.

steps.reason: Only the limited company combines limited liability with separate identity.
steps.result: The answer is C, limited liability company.

content.question: A group of traders wants to own a shop for mutual benefit and share profits to members. Identify the suitable form and state two features it must satisfy.
hints: Ask whether the owners are members seeking mutual benefit rather than outside investors.
That points to a cooperative society owned by its members.
It must pool contributions, vote democratically and use surplus for members.

content.heading: Go deeper: Finding the right form for the task
paragraphs: No form is best in the abstract; the task decides. A market stall that needs little capital suits a sole trader, while a bakery that needs loans, a delivery van and imported equipment needs the borrowing power of a limited company. The choice should weigh how much capital is required against how much liability the owner can carry.

Continuity and control pull in the same direction. A sole trader decides alone but the business trembles when illness strikes. A partnership balances control with shared skill, yet a dispute can dissolve it. A company separates ownership from daily management through directors, so the business survives owners who sell or die.

Public corporations and cooperatives answer a different question. They are chosen when service or mutual benefit matters more than private profit. A cooperative society in a town pools savings to lend to members, while a public corporation supplies a service the market would neglect. JAMB options therefore test purpose as much as size.
bullets: Match capital and liability needs to the form that can bear them.
Continuity rises from sole trader to partnership to company, while control falls.
Purpose selects cooperatives and public corporations when benefit or service dominates.

content.heading: Go deeper: Winding up: dissolution and liquidation
paragraphs: Dissolution is the ending of a partnership or sole business by agreement, death, bankruptcy or notice. The partners settle accounts among themselves, collect debts and divide what remains. Because it ends an internal arrangement, dissolution can be quick, though a court may intervene when partners disagree.

Liquidation is different because a company has a legal life of its own. Winding up follows steps: a liquidator is appointed, assets are sold, creditors are paid in order of priority and any surplus goes to shareholders. A solvent company may be wound up voluntarily, while an insolvent one is compulsorily wound up under court supervision.

Registration is the doorway to this process. Without Corporate Affairs Commission registration, a business remains the owner personally, and winding up is simply settling private debts. With registration, the company can be wound up only through the company law, and the liquidator accounts for every asset and liability. That is why textbooks pair the two terms.
bullets: Dissolution ends the internal partnership or sole arrangement, often by agreement.
Liquidation sells a company's assets to pay creditors under legal supervision.
Registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission is what makes liquidation a legal procedure.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the state keeps enterprises
paragraphs: Some services are natural monopolies because duplicating a network wastes resources. Electricity grids, water mains and ports need single systems that serve whole districts. Private firms might charge high prices or serve only profitable areas, so government ownership aims to extend supply and keep tariffs within reach.

Control of resources adds a second reason. Petroleum, solid minerals and major land assets shape national revenue and security, so the state retains a stake to regulate use. Public ownership also pursues employment, regional balance and industrialisation, backing firms in areas where private capital is thin.

The PHCN heritage shows the tension. Government held electricity to guarantee access, but underfunding, losses and poor service drew criticism. A public enterprise can therefore serve the public in law yet fail in practice, which is why reform debates ask about regulation, funding and management rather than ownership alone. For examinations, keep the reasons separate from the performance.
bullets: Natural monopoly economics favours one network serving all districts at fair tariffs.
Resource control and national revenue justify a state stake in key sectors.
Employment and regional development add reasons beyond profit and efficiency, especially in thinly served areas.

lessons.title: Trade
lessons.objective: Compare the types of retail trade, identify the functions of retailers, classify modern retailing practices, explain the success or failure of retail trade, classify types of wholesalers and discuss the functions and merits or demerits of the middleman.

content.heading: Trade
paragraphs: Trade moves goods from producers to final users by buying in bulk and selling in smaller quantities. Home trade covers retail and wholesale channels inside Nigeria, balancing bulk-breaking against convenience, credit and range for buyers.

content.heading: Itinerant, fixed, departmental and chain shops
paragraphs: At Wuse Market a hawker pushes a cart of phone chargers from bus stop to bus stop, while across the road a fixed shop keeps shelves filled all day. The hawker is itinerant trade, moving to the customer with little capital. The fixed shop waits for the customer, keeping wider stock and a reliable address.

A departmental store under one roof sells many lines through separate departments with common management, while a chain store repeats the same standard shop in several towns. Supermarkets resemble chain stores but carry a wide food and household range under one organisation. Each step adds capital, management and range, but reduces personal attention.
bullets: Itinerant retail has low capital and mobility; fixed retail has stability and wider range.
Departmental and chain retail offer one-stop choice under central control.
Retailers buy in bulk and sell in small quantities to final users.
content.takeaway: Itinerant moves to buyers; fixed, departmental and chain stores organise range centrally.

check.question: A trader moves from street to street selling phone chargers with small capital. Which retail type is that?
check.why: Itinerant trade moves to the buyer with little capital; the others keep fixed premises.

content.heading: What retailers do and why some fail
paragraphs: A retailer at Balogun Market keeps small packets of rice, soap and oil so buyers need not hold a whole bale. She grades goods, stores them until demand appears, offers informal credit and tells buyers how to use the goods. These duties create place, time and possession utility for households with small budgets.

Modern retailing changes how those duties are performed. Branding labels goods so buyers recognise origin and quality, self-service lets shoppers pick goods without waiting for a clerk, vending machines sell at any hour, and luncheon or fuel vouchers let employers pay staff in goods or credit. The functions remain, but the organisation of selling changes.
bullets: Advantages: convenience, small quantities, personal service, credit and choice close to buyers.
Disadvantages: higher price per unit, narrow range and high rent per sale.
Success needs good site, adequate capital, suitable stock, fair pricing and stock control.
Failure follows poor location, weak records, wrong stock, strong competition or costly credit.
content.takeaway: Retailers add convenience by breaking bulk; success needs site, capital and stock control.

check.question: Which practice lets shoppers pick goods without waiting for a clerk?
check.why: Self-service lets buyers choose goods themselves; branding labels them and vending dispenses them.

content.heading: Wholesalers, channels and the middleman
paragraphs: A wholesaler in Onitsha buys a container of shoes at Apapa port and sells pairs to twelve shops. She is a merchant wholesaler because she buys, owns and resells the goods, while an agent only introduces buyers and sellers for commission. A general wholesaler carries many lines, whereas a specialised one carries few lines in depth.

Channels link producer to consumer directly or through wholesalers, agents and retailers, with each link adding service and cost. A wholesaler buys in bulk, stores, grades and breaks bulk, finances retailers and bears risk. That service earns a margin, yet the middleman can also raise price, delay sale and weaken control.
bullets: Merchant wholesalers own goods and bear risk; agents work for commission without ownership.
Merits of middlemen include bulk-breaking, storage, finance, wider reach and steady supply.
Demerits include extra margins, delays, weaker producer control and possible excess profit.
content.takeaway: Wholesalers break bulk and finance trade; each extra link adds service and cost.

check.question: An agent introduces buyers and sellers for commission without owning goods. What is the agent?
check.why: Ownership decides the type: merchants own goods, agents only earn commission.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Name who owns the goods: merchant wholesalers own them, agents do not. A vending machine is automated retail, not itinerant trade. Vouchers pay staff, while branding identifies origin; do not swap these trends in the hall.

content.problem: Which organisation with the same shop in ten towns is chain retail? A. Itinerant B. Fixed shop C. Chain store D. Departmental store

steps.reason: Chain stores repeat the same shop under one organisation
steps.result: Look for many towns with the same standard.

steps.reason: Itinerant moves and fixed stays in one place
steps.result: Only the repeated towns fit the definition.

steps.reason: Ten towns under one control match chain retail
steps.result: The answer is C, chain store.

content.question: A student sells snacks from a weekend stall near a school gate and takes the goods home each night. Is this itinerant or fixed retail? Name two retailer functions and one factor for success.
hints: Ask whether the trader keeps a fixed address or moves to the buyer.
Retailers store goods, break bulk and inform buyers about use.
Site, capital and suitable stock decide if the stall can last.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why a well-kept shop can still fail
paragraphs: A shop can be neat yet empty because its site draws the wrong footfall. A premium bakery near a low-income bus park may win attention but not repeat sales. Rent, lighting and transport must be paid from a thin mark-up on small packets, so the arithmetic fails before the stock does.

Capital decides how long a retailer can wait. A grocer who sells on credit must still pay for new stock at once, and a slow turnover leaves cash locked in sacks that may spoil. Chain stores ease this pressure with central buying and faster stock rotation, while a lone shop depends on its own records and discipline.

Management turns capital into sales through assortment, pricing and service. Too narrow a range loses the one-stop shopper, while too wide a range breeds waste and confusion. Government action also matters: dearer credit, higher rents or a new rival in the same street can close a shop that once traded well.
bullets: Site and catchment income decide whether customers can buy repeatedly.
Working capital and turnover decide whether cash returns before stock rots.
Assortment, pricing and records turn capital into steady sales.

content.heading: Go deeper: Channel length and the middleman debate
paragraphs: A maker of bottled water in Ibadan may sell directly to offices by van, through a wholesaler to shops, or through an agent to distant grocers. Each route is a channel, and its length names the number of independent middlemen between maker and final buyer. A longer channel reaches more outlets, while a shorter one keeps more margin and control.

Middlemen exist because producers cannot economically serve thousands of small buyers alone. A wholesaler consolidates orders, breaks bulk, holds stock near buyers and extends credit in small sums that banks will not risk. Remove that link and the producer must finance vans, warehouses and collectors, usually at higher cost for small lots.

Who pays is the exam test. When each link adds a service, price rises for a reason; when a link adds only delay and a toll, buyers seek a shorter channel. That is why exclusive control over a market can lift margins beyond the cost of the service, and why competition, not abolition, is the usual remedy for excess profit.
bullets: Direct channels keep control; longer channels widen reach but share margin and control.
Middlemen earn margin for consolidation, storage, finance and risk, not for existence alone.
Excess margins signal weak competition rather than proof that middlemen are useless.

content.heading: Go deeper: Branding, self-service and vouchers at work
paragraphs: Branding turns an anonymous good into a promise that can be recognised again. A bag of rice with a registered mark tells the buyer which mill packed it, while an unmarked sack must be trusted on the spot. That mark allows advertising, standards and repeat purchase, and it lets a producer charge for quality rather than for weight alone.

Self-service moves the work of showing goods from the clerk to the shopper. Customers walk the shelves, compare prices and carry baskets to the till, which cuts queuing and lets a store serve more people with fewer staff. Vending machines go further: they sell without any staff, at any hour, for goods that need no advice.

Luncheon and fuel vouchers link an employer to a shop. The firm buys bulk credit for staff, the shop receives guaranteed sales, and the worker chooses food or fuel within the limit. The gain is steady demand and control of spending, while the limit itself shapes where the worker can trade.
bullets: Branding identifies origin and supports quality control and repeat purchase.
Self-service and vending cut staff cost but suit goods needing little advice.
Vouchers give employers control and traders linked, steady demand.

lessons.title: Foreign Trade
lessons.objective: Compare the types of foreign trade, analyse balance of trade and balance of payments, explain the procedures and documents used in foreign trade, identify barriers and tariffs, identify tools for trade restriction and export promotion, and appraise the role of government agencies in foreign trade.

content.heading: Foreign trade
paragraphs: Foreign trade moves goods across national borders for payment in foreign currency. Imports bring goods into Nigeria, exports send them out, and entrepôt trade passes them through. Its cost, paperwork and rules shape prices for every trader.

content.heading: Imports, exports and entrepôt trade
paragraphs: A Lagos importer clears a container of rice at Apapa port for sale in Nigeria, which is an import. A cocoa dealer ships beans from Tin Can port to a buyer in the Netherlands, which is an export. Entrepôt is different: goods enter Nigeria only to be re-exported without sale to a Nigerian buyer.

The balance of trade records only visible goods: exports of goods minus imports of goods over a period. The balance of payments is wider: current account goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts. A country may sell more services than it imports yet still show a poor goods balance.
bullets: Favourable balance of trade means exports of goods exceed imports of goods.
