Balance of payments covers goods, services, income, transfers and capital flows.
Rule: goods only means trade; all current and capital flows means payments.
content.takeaway: Balance of trade counts goods; balance of payments counts goods, services and capital.

check.question: A country exports goods worth 9 and imports goods worth 7. What is the balance of trade?
check.why: Exports 9 minus imports 7 give surplus 2, which is favourable.

content.heading: Paperwork at the port
paragraphs: An importer in Apapa gathers the bill of lading, which proves a carrier has shipped the goods, and the certificate of origin, which shows where they were produced. A consular invoice helps the destination country value the goods for duty. Without these papers, customs cannot release the container.

Payment is secured through the bill of exchange, a written order to pay a sum on a date, and the letter of credit, a bank promise to pay the seller if papers are correct. The letter shifts risk from the importer to a bank. Both documents turn promised payment into a trade instrument.
bullets: Bill of lading is the shipping receipt and title document for goods at sea.
Certificate of origin proves production place; consular invoice aids valuation for duty.
Letter of credit protects the exporter; bill of exchange orders the importer to pay.
content.takeaway: Shipping papers prove movement; payment papers secure the price.

check.question: Which document shows the carrier has shipped the goods and can transfer title at sea?
check.why: The bill of lading is the shipping receipt and title document; the others prove origin, valuation or payment.

content.heading: Barriers, tariffs and help at the border
paragraphs: A government may charge a tariff, a tax on import or export at the border, or set a quota, a fixed maximum quantity allowed in. An embargo bans a named trade completely, while an import licence requires prior permission before goods may enter. Each tool limits foreign goods to protect local producers or raise revenue.

Restriction tools also include exchange controls, duties and standards that raise cost or delay entry. Export promotion uses subsidies, tax relief, trade fairs and market information to lower cost abroad. The Nigeria Customs Service collects duties and blocks smuggling, the Nigerian Ports Authority runs ports and channels, and the Nigerian Export Promotion Council supports exporters.
bullets: Tariffs raise revenue, protect infant industries and deter dumping of cheap foreign goods.
Quotas fix quantity; embargoes ban trade; licences control who may import.
Agencies: Customs for duty and control, Ports Authority for ports, NEPC for exporters.
content.takeaway: Tariffs tax entry; quotas, bans and licences limit it; agencies police it.

check.question: A government fixes the maximum quantity of rice that may enter from abroad. Which tool is that?
check.why: A quota fixes quantity; a tariff taxes entry and an embargo bans trade.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the question names goods only, choose balance of trade. If it names services, income or capital flows, choose balance of payments. A tariff is a price tool; a quota is a quantity tool.

content.problem: A country exports goods worth 9 and imports goods worth 7. What is the balance of trade? A. Deficit 2 B. Surplus 2 C. Surplus 16 D. Deficit 16

steps.reason: Balance of trade counts goods only
steps.result: Use exports minus imports of goods.

steps.reason: Exports exceed imports, so the result is positive
A positive goods surplus is favourable

content.question: A cocoa exporter ships beans from Tin Can port, sends a bill of lading and a certificate of origin, and is paid under a letter of credit. Name the trade type and one document, and state why the credit helps the exporter.
hints: The beans move outward from Nigeria to pay abroad.
The bill of lading proves shipment and titles goods at sea.
The bank pays on clean papers, so the seller need not trust a distant buyer.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why payments matter beyond goods
paragraphs: Goods that can be seen at a port are visible trade, but services are invisible: shipping, insurance, tourism and banking earned abroad change a nation's receipts without crossing a quay. A country that imports many shipping and insurance services pays abroad even when its goods surplus looks steady. The balance of payments catches that payment because it counts services alongside goods.

The current account records goods, services, income and transfers, while the capital and financial accounts record purchases of assets and changes in reserves. A persistent current deficit is financed by borrowing or by selling assets, and markets may then press the exchange rate. That is why central banks watch both accounts, not the goods balance alone.

Counter trade answers the same need for payment when cash is scarce. In counter-purchase, the importer agrees that goods will be bought back, and in a barter deal goods are exchanged for goods. The device keeps trade moving, but valuation and quality disputes make it costlier than an ordinary money sale through a port such as Apapa.
bullets: Visible trade is goods at the port; invisible trade is services and income.
A current deficit must be financed by borrowing, asset sales or reserves.
Counter trade replaces cash with reciprocal purchase or barter at higher cost.

content.heading: Go deeper: How shipping and payment papers work together
paragraphs: The bill of lading is more than a receipt. As a receipt it shows the carrier has taken the goods, as evidence it states the contract terms, and as a document of title it can transfer ownership while goods are still at sea. A buyer who holds an order bill can sell the cargo to another buyer before the ship docks.

Origin and consular papers guard revenue and honesty. The certificate of origin tells customs where goods were made, so the correct duty and any preference can be applied, while the consular invoice, certified by the importer country's consul, declares value and description for assessment. Together they stop undervaluation and smuggling that would otherwise undercut lawful traders.

The letter of credit and the bill of exchange divide risk between buyer, seller and bank. Under a credit, the buyer's bank promises to pay only when it receives clean papers, so the seller need not trust a distant buyer, while the bill of exchange, when drawn on the buyer and accepted, becomes a tradable order to pay. Both turn trust into paperwork that a bank can check.
bullets: Bill of lading is receipt, contract evidence and transferable title at sea.
Origin and consular papers fix duty and block undervaluation and smuggling.
Letter of credit pays on clean papers; bill of exchange orders payment.

content.heading: Go deeper: Barriers, promotion and the agencies at work
paragraphs: Governments restrict trade for reasons beyond revenue. A tariff can give a new factory time to learn, a quota can save scarce currency, and a ban can guard health or security. Each tool raises the price for the local buyer, who pays for protection that the producer enjoys, and trading partners may also answer with duties of their own, so protection can narrow the market it meant to help.

At the border the agencies divide labour. The Nigeria Customs Service checks papers, assesses duty, prevents smuggling and collects revenue for government, while the Nigerian Ports Authority owns and operates port infrastructure for Apapa, Tin Can, Onne and other ports, so ships and cargo move safely. The Nigerian Export Promotion Council helps exporters find buyers, meet standards and join trade fairs.

Promotion and restriction are opposite hands of the same policy. Exchange controls and high duties hold back imports, while export credits, tax relief and market information push goods out. A trader meets both at once: the same port that checks an import levy may load an export that the promotion council helped to market, and that balance decides whether foreign trade widens choice or merely raises cost.
bullets: Infant, revenue, health and security aims explain most barriers.
Customs controls and collects; Ports Authority operates; NEPC promotes exports.
Deterring imports while aiding exports is the same policy in opposite hands.

lessons.title: Purchase and Sale of Goods
lessons.objective: Examine the procedures and documents used in the purchase and sale of goods, determine the terms of trade, distinguish between cash and credit forms of payment, explain the meaning and types of credit, analyse the merits and demerits of credit transactions, and identify the means of payment.

content.heading: Purchase and sale of goods
paragraphs: Goods move through enquiry, order and invoice, on agreed terms of trade, and are settled in cash or on credit by a recognised means of payment.

content.heading: From enquiry to statement of accounts
paragraphs: A trader in Onitsha wants 500 cartons of oil from a mill in Kano. She sends an enquiry asking for availability and terms, and the seller replies with a quotation stating price, quality and delivery.

She places an order, a firm instruction to supply, and the seller issues an invoice, a bill showing goods supplied and amount owed. A proforma invoice is similar but sent before dispatch as an estimate, while the statement of accounts lists all transactions and balances due.

For imports, the indent is the order sent through an agent abroad, the consular invoice is certified by the consul, and the bill of lading is the shipping receipt and title document. The certificate of origin proves where goods were made, and the consignment note records dispatch by road, rail or air.
bullets: An enquiry asks; a quotation offers; an order instructs supply.
An invoice demands payment; a proforma invoice estimates before dispatch.
Foreign documents prove origin and shipment for customs and banks.
content.takeaway: Enquiry, order and invoice carry goods from request to payment.

check.question: A seller sends a document before dispatch showing estimated charges for agreement. What is it?
check.why: A proforma invoice estimates before dispatch, while an invoice demands payment after supply.

content.heading: Terms of trade and payment
paragraphs: A trader in Aba buys 100 bales of cloth. A trade discount is taken off list price for traders, a quantity discount rewards bulk buying, and a cash discount rewards prompt payment. A warranty is the seller's promise to repair or replace faulty goods.

In foreign trade, C.O.D. means cash on delivery and E.O.E. means errors and omissions excepted. F.O.B., free on board, means the seller delivers on board the ship, while C.I.F., cost, insurance and freight, means those three charges are included in the price.

Spot or prompt payment means paying at once, while credit means buying now and paying later. Credit types include trade credit, bank credit and bills of exchange; it funds purchases and smooths cash flow but risks bad debts and higher prices.
bullets: Trade discount goes to traders; cash discount rewards prompt payment.
Credit finances purchases and supports higher turnover.
Credit tempts overtrading and risks bad debts and higher prices.
content.takeaway: Discounts cut price, trade codes settle foreign costs, and credit defers payment.

check.question: Which discount rewards a buyer for paying promptly?
check.why: Cash discount rewards prompt payment, while trade discount goes to traders and quantity discount rewards bulk buying.

content.heading: Means of payment
paragraphs: A market woman in Ibadan receives naira notes and coins as legal tender, which a court must accept. She may pay by cheque, a written order on her bank, or a standing order, a regular instruction to pay. A bank draft is a bank's promise to pay and suits a new supplier.

For small sums, postal orders and money orders move value without a bank account. A bill of exchange orders a drawer to pay another, while a promissory note is the maker's promise to pay. Both can be discounted at a bank.

A mail transfer or telegraphic transfer moves funds by post or wire, while traveller's cheques let travellers pay abroad. Today a POS agent takes e-payment by transfer, card or USSD, and a recharge card gives airtime value that traders resell.
bullets: Legal tender must be accepted; cheques draw on an account.
Bills order another to pay; notes promise payment.
Transfers move funds across distance; e-payment settles instantly by phone or card.
content.takeaway: Cash, cheques, transfers and e-payment move money with different safeguards.

check.question: A buyer instructs her bank to pay monthly in fixed amounts without signing each time. Which means is that?
check.why: A standing order is a regular instruction to pay, while a bank draft is a single payment promise.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Trade discount comes off list price before cash discount, so apply trade discount first and cash discount on the reduced balance. A proforma invoice is never a demand for payment; only an invoice demands payment.

content.problem: A trader buys goods listed at ₦200,000 with 10% trade discount and 5% cash discount for prompt payment. What is the amount payable?

steps.reason: Trade discount comes off list price first to get net trade price
Cash discount is calculated on the reduced balance after trade discount
Subtract cash discount to get final amount owed

content.question: Goods listed at ₦150,000 attract 20% trade discount and 5% cash discount for prompt payment. What is the amount payable?
hints: Deduct trade discount from list price first.
Calculate cash discount on the reduced balance.
Subtract the cash discount to find the payable amount.

content.heading: Go deeper: Foreign trade documents and why customs insists on paper
paragraphs: Foreign trade adds brokers, carriers, insurers and customs officers between buyer and seller. The indent remains the foreign order, but it now travels through an indent agent who sources goods, checks quality and arranges shipment. That agent turns a vague request into a priced, shippable offer.

The bill of lading is therefore more than a receipt. It is the contract of carriage, the receipt for goods shipped, and, if marked to order, a title document that can be transferred. A consignment note differs because it records dispatch by road, rail or air without conferring the same title.

The consular invoice and certificate of origin answer two customs questions: what is the value and where was it made. The consul certifies the invoice value, while chambers of commerce or manufacturers certify origin. Both protect revenue and stop false claims for preference.

A trader who keeps this chain complete clears goods faster and borrows more easily. A bank lending against an F.O.B. shipment will ask for the bill of lading, an approved indent and a certified invoice before it releases funds. Paper is therefore not bureaucracy but collateral.
bullets: An indent agent converts a request into a priced offer.
A bill of lading can be title; a consignment note cannot.
Consular invoice proves value; certificate of origin proves source.

content.heading: Go deeper: F.O.B. versus C.I.F. and who carries the risk
paragraphs: F.O.B. and C.I.F. look like pricing codes but they decide who pays for freight, insurance and risk. Under F.O.B., free on board, the seller's duty ends when goods are on board the ship. Under C.I.F., cost, insurance and freight, the seller pays for carriage and insurance to the named port, though risk may still pass earlier.

The distinction matters because cost and risk do not always move together. A C.I.F. buyer benefits from a single price but must still insure or claim once goods are at risk. An F.O.B. buyer chooses her own carrier and insurer, gaining control but carrying the burden of arranging carriage.

Examiners often test the edge case where goods are lost at sea. Under F.O.B., the buyer bears loss after shipment and must still pay. Under C.I.F., the seller has paid freight and insurance but the buyer still bears property risk unless the contract says otherwise.

C.O.D. and E.O.E. prevent similar traps at a smaller scale. Cash on delivery protects a seller who fears default by demanding payment when goods arrive. Errors and omissions excepted protects a seller who made a clerical mistake on an invoice, while the buyer must still prove the claim for correction.
bullets: F.O.B. puts freight and insurance on the buyer.
C.I.F. puts freight and insurance in the seller's price.
Risk can pass before cost; read contract, not price.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cash, credit and modern payment in Nigeria
paragraphs: Cash and credit differ not only in timing but in risk, because cash includes notes, coins and instant electronic settlement and closes the debt at once. Credit leaves a promise outstanding: trade credit, bank overdraft or a bill of exchange. That promise must be secured by records, reputation and a due date.

Bills of exchange and promissory notes turn that promise into a tradable instrument. A drawee who accepts a bill becomes liable to pay, and a holder can discount it at a bank before maturity. The discount fee is the price of turning future money into present cash.

Modern means have not removed these problems; they have moved them. A cheque can be dishonoured for insufficient funds, a transfer can go to a wrong account, and a recharge card loses value if airtime expires. POS agents and e-payment reduce cash-carrying risk but add network failure and fraud alerts.

A trader therefore matches means to risk and distance. Standing orders suit rent and salaries, bank drafts suit new suppliers, and telegraphic or mail transfers suit distant buyers. The right choice is the one whose promise the other side can enforce without added cost.
bullets: Cash closes the debt; credit creates an enforceable promise.
A discounted bill buys present cash at a fee.
E-payment removes cash risk but adds network and fraud risk.

lessons.title: Financing Business
lessons.objective: Identify the ways of financing a business, discuss the different types of capital, compute the different forms of capital, profits and turnover, appraise the problems associated with sourcing finances for business, and assess the role of Bureau de change in an economy.

content.heading: Financing business
paragraphs: A business needs money to start and grow, raised from savings, shares, loans and profit, held as different forms of capital, and spent in the face of shortage.

content.heading: Ways of raising finance
paragraphs: A young trader in Kano starts with personal savings, her own money ring-fenced for the shop. She may also sell shares, part-ownership in a company, or bonds, loans raised from the public. To sell shares she must register with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC).

A bank loan and a debenture, a loan secured on company assets, give larger sums at fixed interest. A mortgage loans money against land or buildings, while a bank overdraft lets a current account fall negative up to an agreed limit.

Credit purchase lets her take machines now and pay in instalments, and leasing hires machines for rent with an option to buy. Ploughing back of profit keeps earnings inside the firm as dividends foregone. That retained profit needs no interest and no security.
bullets: Shares give ownership; bonds and debentures are loans to repay.
Mortgages need property; overdrafts suit short, fluctuating needs.
Leasing hires assets; ploughing back retains profit inside.
content.takeaway: Owners, lenders and retained profit finance the firm at different costs.

check.question: Which source uses money already earned and kept in the firm?
check.why: Ploughing back retains profit inside instead of paying dividends, while the others borrow from outside.

content.heading: Forms of capital
paragraphs: Share capital is money from issuing shares. Authorized capital is the maximum a registered company may issue, while issued capital is the part offered to the public. Called-up capital is what shareholders are asked to pay, and paid-up capital is what they have actually paid.

Capital owned and owners' equity are the owners' stake: assets minus liabilities. Liquid capital is cash and near-cash assets that can pay debts quickly. Working capital is what remains for daily trading after short-term debts are met.

Turnover is total sales value for the period. Gross profit is turnover minus cost of sales, and net profit is gross profit minus all expenses. Those two profit figures show earning power, while the capital ladder shows how much was raised and paid.
bullets: Authorized is the limit; issued is offered; paid-up is paid.
Equity is assets minus liabilities owned by owners.
Gross profit is turnover less cost; net profit less expenses.
content.takeaway: Authorized to paid-up narrows down; equity and working capital sustain trade.

check.question: A company may issue up to ₦5 million but offers ₦3 million and receives ₦2 million. What is paid-up capital?
check.why: Paid-up capital is what shareholders have actually paid, not the limit or the amount offered.

content.heading: Problems and the Bureau de change
paragraphs: Small traders face high interest, demand for collateral, short repayment periods and strict bank records. New firms without track records, traders without property titles and businesses in volatile markets therefore struggle, even when the project is sound.

The Bureau de change, licensed in markets and streets, buys and sells foreign currency for importers and travellers. It helps a trader pay a foreign supplier and gives small firms a channel where banks may not reach. It also supplies cash for travel and foreign fees.

Those problems explain why internal finance and leasing matter: they avoid collateral and interest. A firm that keeps records, registers with CAC and repays promptly reduces its cost of finance over time.
bullets: High cost, collateral and records block small firms.
Bureaux supply foreign currency where bank access is thin.
Good records and prompt repayment lower future cost.
content.takeaway: Scarce finance raises cost; Bureaux ease foreign payment access.

check.question: Why does a trader buy dollars from a market Bureau de change?
check.why: Bureaux buy and sell foreign currency for importers, while registration, mortgages and shares concern other institutions.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Never confuse authorized capital, which is the legal limit, with paid-up capital, which is money actually received. Turnover shows sales, gross profit shows margin after cost of sales, and net profit shows what remains after all expenses.

content.problem: A shop has turnover of ₦3,500,000, cost of sales of ₦2,200,000 and expenses of ₦800,000. Calculate gross profit and net profit.

steps.reason: Gross profit is turnover minus cost of sales
Net profit is gross profit minus all expenses
Net profit is the final earning after all deductions

content.question: A bakery has turnover ₦2,400,000, cost of sales ₦1,500,000 and expenses ₦600,000. Find gross and net profit.
hints: Subtract cost of sales from turnover for gross profit.
Subtract all expenses from gross profit for net profit.
Check that net profit is smaller than gross profit.

content.heading: Go deeper: Internal, external, short and long finance
paragraphs: The first distinction is who supplies the money. Internal finance comes from the firm itself: personal savings and ploughing back of profit, while external finance comes from others: shares, bonds, loans, debentures and overdrafts. Internal money is cheaper but limited by earnings, while external money is larger but must be repaid or shared.

The second distinction is time. Short finance lasts months, including overdrafts, trade credit and credit purchase for stock, while long finance funds years of shares, debentures, mortgages and leasing for machines and buildings. Mismatching them, such as funding a permanent shop with an overdraft, creates repayment pressure.

Leasing and credit purchase show why form matters more than label. Leasing gives use of a machine for rent without ownership until exercise of the option, while credit purchase gives ownership on instalments but ties the firm to a creditor. Both spread cost, yet they differ in control and risk.

A Niger Delta equipment firm therefore chooses a portfolio, not a single source. It retains profit for deposits, leases one machine, and seeks a mortgage for the premises, with each choice balancing cost, security and control. The exam test is whether the pictured source fits that balance.
bullets: Internal is owned; external is borrowed or shared.
Short funds stock; long funds premises and machines.
Leasing rents use; credit purchase buys in instalments.

content.heading: Go deeper: From authorized to paid-up and profit to turnover
paragraphs: The capital ladder narrows at each step, from authorized capital as the ceiling in the memorandum, say ₦5 million, to issued capital as the slice offered, say ₦3 million. Called-up capital is the slice the directors request, say ₦2.5 million, while paid-up capital is the slice received, say ₦2 million. Only the last is cash in the bank.

Working capital and liquid capital answer different questions, because working capital is current assets minus current liabilities as the buffer that keeps buying and paying. Liquid capital is cash plus assets convertible in days. A firm can own equity yet fail if working capital turns negative and suppliers refuse terms.

Profit must be read with turnover, because gross profit compares turnover with cost of sales and shows pricing power on goods. Net profit subtracts rent, wages, interest and other expenses and shows what owners keep. A high turnover with low net profit signals tight margins or bloated costs, not success.

A Lagos fabric shop illustrates the full chain, where it issues capital to stock bales, turns stock into turnover, and converts turnover into gross profit after cost. If rent and wages consume that profit, net profit stays small. Lenders therefore ask for both statements: capital shows backing, profit shows flow.
bullets: Only paid-up capital is cash; authorized is a ceiling.
Working capital sustains daily trade; liquid capital pays quickly.
Turnover shows scale; net profit shows earning.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why small firms struggle and how Bureaux help
paragraphs: Sourcing finance is hard because lenders ration risk. A bank with limited funds prefers borrowers with property, audited records and a steady sales history. A first-time trader with no title document, no CAC registration and no bank statement cannot prove repayment, so the lender either refuses or charges more.

Costs then compound because high interest raises break-even sales and short tenors force fast turnover. Delay in approval misses market windows, while collateral demands expose family property. Informal money is faster but carries higher rates and social pressure, so each problem has a different cause: information, security, time and price.

The Bureau de change eases one part of this squeeze: access to foreign currency. A fabric importer who cannot open a domiciliary account can still buy dollars for fabric or pay a supplier through a licensed bureau in the market. That keeps the supply chain moving despite thin bank access.

Bureaux do not solve borrowing problems, and they carry their own risks of fake notes and rate swings. A prudent trader compares rates, checks licences and keeps receipts. The durable fix remains wider: registration, records, savings and prompt repayment that build a credit history.
bullets: Lenders ration scarce funds by records and security.
Bureaux supply currency, not credit or collateral.
Records and repayment build credit history over time.

lessons.title: Aids to Trade
lessons.objective: Explain the meaning and role of advertising and identify its media and methods; categorise the types of bank and assess their services and challenges, including e-banking; analyse the types and merits or demerits of communication, including courier and GSM contributions, and outline barriers to communication.

content.heading: Aids to Trade
paragraphs: Trade needs services that move information, money and messages between buyers and sellers. Advertising, banking and communication are three aids that make exchange possible across distance and time.

content.heading: Advertising: telling buyers about goods
paragraphs: A producer in Onitsha makes sandals that traders in Kano have never seen. Without information, the sandals remain unsold and buyers remain unaware. Advertising is any paid communication that informs and persuades buyers about a product.

Its roles are to create awareness, induce demand, promote goodwill and support sales. Types include informative, persuasive and reminder advertising, delivered through media such as newspapers, radio, television, posters and the internet. Methods include press, broadcast, outdoor and direct advertising, each chosen for reach and cost.

Advantages include wider markets, faster feedback and support for new products. Disadvantages include high cost, exaggeration that misleads buyers and competition that may clutter messages. It is not personal selling, which is paid face-to-face persuasion, nor publicity, which is unpaid news coverage.
bullets: Advertising is paid communication that informs and persuades buyers
Media include press, radio, television, posters and internet
It widens markets but costs money and can mislead
content.takeaway: Advertising is paid persuasion that creates awareness and demand through chosen media.

check.question: A firm pays for a radio jingle to persuade buyers. What is this?
check.why: Paid persuasive communication to buyers through media is advertising, while publicity is unpaid coverage.

content.heading: Banks: types, services and e-banking
paragraphs: A trader in Apapa receives payment from a customer in Sokoto without carrying cash. She deposits the money through a branch and checks it by phone at night. A bank is an institution that accepts deposits and lends money.

Types include commercial banks, merchant banks, development banks and microfinance banks. Commercial banks serve the public with deposits and loans, while merchant banks mainly finance large projects and do not take savings. Services include current and savings accounts, transfers, loans, foreign exchange and safe custody, while e-banking offers internet, mobile and card services.

Challenges include fraud, network failure, high charges and rural access problems. E-banking helps speed and convenience but cannot replace cash where networks fail. A commercial bank takes deposits from the public, while a merchant bank does not, so they are not the same.
bullets: Commercial banks take public deposits; merchant banks finance projects
E-banking covers internet, mobile and card transactions
Fraud, network failure and rural access limit banking services
content.takeaway: Banks take deposits and lend money, while e-banking speeds transactions.

check.question: Which bank mainly finances large projects and does not accept public deposits?
check.why: Merchant banks finance large projects and do not take public deposits, unlike commercial banks.

content.heading: Communication: carrying messages between traders
paragraphs: A seller in Yaba needs to confirm an order with a buyer in Port Harcourt. He writes the order, sends it quickly and receives a reply the same day. Communication is the process of sending and receiving information to support trade decisions.

The procedure moves from sender to message, channel, receiver and feedback. Types include letters, telephone, telex, radio, television, courier services and GSM mobile phones. Courier delivers documents physically within set time, while GSM sends voice and messages electronically without moving paper.

Trends include mobile banking alerts, internet messaging and electronic transfer of documents, which speed trade. Merits include speed, accuracy and wider reach, while demerits include cost and failure during network breakdown. Barriers include poor infrastructure, language differences, illiteracy and insecurity along routes.
bullets: Sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback complete communication
Courier moves documents physically; GSM moves voice electronically
Poor infrastructure, language and illiteracy block communication
content.takeaway: Communication carries trade information by courier, GSM and other channels fast.

check.question: A signed contract must move from Lagos to Abuja within a day. Which aid best suits it?
check.why: Courier services deliver original documents within set time, while GSM sends voice without moving paper.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In options, first check paid persuasive content. If it is paid and persuasive to buyers, choose advertising. If it is unpaid news, choose publicity. For banks, a public deposit points to a commercial bank.

content.problem: A trader wants many buyers to know a new soap quickly and cheaply across Nigeria. Which aid should be chosen, and why?

steps.reason: The need is wide awareness at low cost, so choose one method
Radio reaches many buyers, including rural listeners, at moderate cost
It creates awareness and induces demand for the soap

content.question: A trader wants to move a signed contract from Lagos to Abuja within one day. Which communication aid should be chosen?
hints: The need is an original document moved in set time
Courier moves documents physically while GSM moves voice electronically
Choose the aid that delivers the original within one day

content.heading: Go deeper: How advertising work is divided between press, broadcast and outdoor
paragraphs: Press advertising in newspapers and magazines gives detailed messages and a lasting record. Readers can study price and quality at their own pace, which suits goods that need explanation. The weakness is that literacy is required and the message may be seen only once.

Broadcast advertising on radio and television speaks to listeners who cannot read and reaches them quickly. Radio is cheap and portable within Nigeria, while television shows the product and builds trust. Both compete with other programmes and can be skipped, so repetition becomes necessary.

Outdoor advertising through posters, billboards and vehicle panels reaches traders in busy markets and motor parks. It gives constant town exposure but cannot carry long details and suffers from weather damage. Direct advertising by letters, flyers and messages targets selected buyers and allows reply, which mass media cannot do well.

The confusable pair is advertising and publicity. Advertising is paid, controlled and repeated by the seller, while publicity is unpaid coverage that the media chooses to publish. An advertisement is therefore certain to appear, while publicity is never guaranteed and may be critical.
bullets: Press details information for literate buyers who can reread
Broadcast reaches illiterate listeners quickly but needs repetition
Outdoor and direct advertising target places and selected buyers

content.heading: Go deeper: How banks earn money and why e-banking still fails
paragraphs: A bank earns from a regular organisation of money. It pays lower interest on deposits and charges higher interest on loans, keeping the spread. Fees for transfers, cards and accounts add income, while staff, branches and technology add cost.
Profit therefore depends on keeping deposits stable and loans sound.

Types reflect different work in that organisation. Commercial banks and community banks accept deposits and finance small trade, while development banks provide long-term funds for agriculture and industry. Merchant banks do not accept public deposits but arrange mergers, issues and large loans.
Choosing the wrong type therefore limits the service available.

E-banking changes access rather than removing risk. Internet and mobile programmes allow transfer, balance enquiry and bill payment without a branch visit. Fraud, wrong transfers and network failure then become the main losses, so passwords, alerts and limits protect accounts.
Cash remains useful when networks fail in rural areas.

Challenges therefore go beyond queues. Weak electricity, poor signals, low digital literacy and staff shortages slow adoption. A bank programme that teaches security and keeps agent points in markets often helps more than a new application alone.
Access improves only when the organisation, the network and the user all work together.
bullets: Banks earn from interest spreads and service fees
E-banking speeds access but adds fraud and network risk
Security, alerts and agent points protect e-banking users

content.heading: Go deeper: Why messages fail and how courier and GSM differ
paragraphs: Communication succeeds only when the receiver understands the message as sent. Noise, distance and poor writing therefore distort orders and cause disagreement. Feedback is the proof that the message was received correctly, so a trader confirms delivery before paying.
The process is thus a two-way agreement, not a single broadcast.

Courier services belong to physical trade because they move the original document. They collect, track and deliver letters and contracts within a promised time across Nigeria. The cost is higher than a call, and speed depends on roads and flights.
GSM belongs to instant trade because it moves voice, text and data electronically without moving paper.

Trends show a move toward mobile and internet channels for speed. Banks send alerts by GSM, while traders share prices by messaging and documents by email. These channels suit confirmation and repeat orders very well.
They still need paper for legal proof, so both methods are used together in serious trade.

Barriers explain the failures that traders meet daily. Poor roads delay couriers, while weak signals delay GSM messages and mobile banking. Language differences and low literacy cause misreading, and insecurity discourages movement of goods and cash.
Each barrier therefore calls for a different remedy rather than more advertising.
bullets: Courier moves original documents; GSM moves voice and text
Feedback confirms that the receiver understood the message
Infrastructure, language and insecurity block trade messages

lessons.title: Insurance, Tourism, Transport and Warehousing
lessons.objective: Describe the types, principles, terms and importance of insurance and identify types of risk; explain the meaning and forms of tourism, its importance, the agencies that promote it in Nigeria and its challenges; appraise the modes, importance and advantages or disadvantages of transportation; highlight the importance of warehousing and evaluate factors that determine the siting of warehouses.

content.heading: Insurance, Tourism, Transport and Warehousing
paragraphs: Goods move and travellers travel while traders bear risk of loss. Insurance, tourism, transport and warehousing manage that risk, movement and storage to support trade across Nigeria.

content.heading: Insurance: spreading the cost of loss
paragraphs: A trader ships yams from Benue to Lagos. Fire destroys part of the stock and the trader bears the full loss. Insurance is a contract that spreads the cost of accidental loss among many policyholders.

Types include life, fire and marine insurance, motor insurance, health cover and agricultural insurance. Each covers a different risk, from death to fire, accident at sea, vehicle damage, illness and crop failure. The cover chosen depends on the loss the trader fears most.

Principles include utmost good faith, insurable interest and indemnity, which restores the insured to the former position. Terms include premium, risk, policy and claim. Insurance matters because it encourages trade, protects assets and spreads loss beyond one firm.
bullets: Fundamental risks affect many people; particular risks affect one person
Pure risks bring only loss; speculative risks bring profit or loss
Premium is the price paid for cover under a policy
Indemnity restores the insured, but does not create profit
content.takeaway: Insurance spreads loss through premiums, on principles of good faith.

check.question: Fire destroys a trader's stock. Which principle limits the payment to the actual loss?
check.why: Indemnity restores the insured to the former position and prevents profit from loss.

content.heading: Tourism: travel for leisure and business
paragraphs: A family travels from Enugu to Obudu to see the hills and cool air. They pay for transport, lodging and guides while away from home. Tourism is travel away from home for leisure, culture or business that brings spending.

Forms include domestic, international, cultural, ecotourism and business tourism. It creates jobs, earns foreign exchange, promotes culture and supports local trade. The Nigerian Tourism Development Corporation, NTDC, promotes destinations and regulates tourism operators across Nigeria.

Challenges include poor infrastructure, insecurity, low promotion and environmental damage. Centres such as Olumo Rock, Yankari National Park and the Obudu plateau attract visitors. Tourism therefore needs security and services to grow.
bullets: Domestic tourism stays within Nigeria; international crosses borders
NTDC promotes destinations and regulates tourism operators
Poor infrastructure and insecurity limit tourist visits
content.takeaway: Tourism earns income for Nigeria but needs security, services and promotion.

check.question: Which agency promotes destinations and regulates tourism operators in Nigeria?
check.why: The Nigerian Tourism Development Corporation, NTDC, promotes destinations and regulates operators.

content.heading: Transport and warehousing: moving and storing goods
paragraphs: A consignment leaves Apapa Port in Lagos for Kano. It may go by lorry, train or ship depending on cost and urgency. Transport is the movement of goods and people from one place to another.

Modes include road, rail, water and air, with air fastest but costly. Road reaches rural markets, while rail and water carry bulk goods cheaply. Warehousing stores goods until needed and breaks bulk for distribution.

Transport links producers to markets and lowers prices, but road congestion, accidents and rail delays raise costs. Warehouses protect goods, smooth supply and support trade. They are sited near markets, ports and roads for access and low running cost.
bullets: Rail and water carry bulk cheaply; air is fast but costly
Road transport reaches rural areas but can congest and crash
Types include private, public and bonded warehouses for storage
Yaba warehouses suit trading access; siting follows markets and ports
content.takeaway: Transport moves goods between markets, while warehouses store and distribute them.

check.question: Heavy bulk goods must move cheaply over a long distance. Which modes suit this best?
check.why: Rail and water carry bulk cheaply over long distances, while air is fast but costly.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For risk, check scope. If many people are affected, choose fundamental risk. If one firm alone is affected, choose particular risk. For agencies, NTDC promotes tourism in Nigeria, while insurers manage risk.

content.problem: A trader insures a lorry load of grain against fire and pays a premium. Fire damages part of the load. What should the trader do next?

steps.reason: The policy states the covered risk and the claim procedure
The trader notifies the insurer with evidence of loss
Indemnity restores the trader to the former position

content.question: A firm stores imported spare parts for quick sale in Yaba. Which reasoning best explains the warehouse site?
hints: Imported goods arrive through Apapa Port and move to Yaba trading
Siting follows markets, ports and roads for access and low cost
Yaba gives trading access, so choose access to markets

content.heading: Go deeper: How insurance principles control the contract
paragraphs: Insurance would collapse without good faith because the insurer depends on the organisation of facts from the insured. The proposer must disclose every material fact, from health to past losses. Concealment therefore allows the insurer to avoid the claim, since the risk priced was not the risk promised.

Insurable interest ensures that insurance does not become gambling. A trader has interest in goods that will raise money, while a stranger has none in those goods. That interest must exist when the contract starts and, for property, when the loss occurs.
Without it, cover is void and payment is refused.

Indemnity prevents profit from loss and keeps cover honest. Fire cover pays the actual loss, so the insured is restored but never enriched. Life cover is the exception because a human life cannot be valued in money.
The rule therefore stops over-insurance from creating a motive to cause loss.

Proximate cause, contribution and subrogation complete the system. Proximate cause asks which peril actually caused the loss, not which events came before it. Contribution shares the claim when the same risk is insured twice, while subrogation lets the insurer pursue the party who caused the loss.
bullets: Good faith requires full disclosure of material facts
Insurable interest stops insurance from becoming gambling
Indemnity restores the insured without creating profit

content.heading: Go deeper: How tourism becomes spending in Nigeria
paragraphs: Tourism earns money because visitors must pay for what they use while away. They pay for coaches, fuel, hotels, food, guides and park fees before they leave. Much of that spending reaches rural hosts who sell crafts and meals.
The benefit therefore spreads beyond the hotel owner to the surrounding market.

Agencies shape that spending through an organised programme. The Nigerian Tourism Development Corporation promotes destinations, sets standards and trains operators. State ministries, the National Park Service and private operators then provide roads, security and services.
A destination without such organisation rarely attracts repeat visits.

Forms of tourism suit different visitors and spending patterns. Domestic tourism brings steady demand from Nigerian families and traders, while international tourism brings foreign exchange and higher hotel spending. Cultural tourism supports festivals and museums, and ecotourism supports parks and reserves.
Each form needs daily management, not only promotion.

Challenges show why promotion alone fails. Poor roads, water and power raise costs, while insecurity frightens visitors and drives spending away. Damage to sites also reduces the attraction that drew the visitor.
Centres such as Yankari and Obudu therefore need access, safety and care to keep their value.
bullets: Visitors pay hotels, transport, food and guides while away
NTDC promotes and regulates tourism operators in Nigeria
Access, safety and site care keep tourist centres attractive

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing transport and warehouse sites
paragraphs: The right mode depends on distance, weight, value and urgency. Water and rail carry heavy bulk cheaply over long distances, while road serves scattered markets with flexible timing. Air carries urgent, light and valuable goods at high cost.
A trader therefore chooses mode by total cost, not by speed alone.

Each mode carries distinct advantages and disadvantages. Road is door to door and reaches rural areas but faces congestion and accidents. Rail and water are cheap for bulk but need terminals and fixed routes, while air avoids roads but needs airports.
The JAMB test is whether the answer names the trade-off, not the mode alone.

Warehousing protects goods while they wait for buyers. Private warehouses belong to firms, public warehouses serve many traders and bonded warehouses hold imported goods under customs control. Their functions include storage, sorting, packing, stock control and breaking bulk.
Yaba warehouses illustrate storage that supports daily trading rather than long hoarding.

Siting follows access and cost. A warehouse near Apapa Port suits importers because goods move from ship to store without long haulage. A site near markets, rail lines and good roads serves many buyers at low transport cost.
Cheap land alone is not enough if lorries cannot reach the site regularly.
bullets: Rail and water suit cheap bulk; air suits urgent valuable goods
Warehouses store, sort, pack and break bulk for traders
Ports, markets and roads decide warehouse locations

lessons.title: Trade Associations
lessons.objective: Discuss the objectives and functions of trade and manufacturer's associations, list the objectives and functions of Chambers of Commerce, and explain the different forms of business combination/merger.

content.heading: Trade associations
paragraphs: Small traders who join together can protect their interests, standardise quality and deal with government as one voice. This lesson explains how trade associations, chambers of commerce and business combinations serve that purpose.

content.heading: Trade and manufacturers' associations
paragraphs: In a Lagos market, garri sellers join a Garri Sellers' Association so that they can speak with one voice. A manufacturer belongs to a manufacturers' association, while a trader belongs to a trade association; the grouping follows the work members do.

Their objectives are to protect members' interests, maintain fair prices and quality, and settle disputes among members. Their functions include collecting market information, regulating entry and conduct, and representing the trade before government and the public. They also organise training, encourage cooperation and run welfare schemes for members, such as the Cocoa Farmers' Association and the Poultry Farmers' Association.
bullets: Objective: protect members, secure fair prices and maintain quality standards.
Function: share information, regulate conduct and represent members to government.
Function: settle disputes, organise training and run welfare for members.
content.takeaway: Trade and manufacturers' associations unite similar traders and producers to protect their interests.

check.question: Which body best fits a group of poultry breeders?
check.why: A poultry association serves poultry farmers; the others serve cocoa, garri or many trades.

content.heading: Chambers of commerce
paragraphs: A new trader in Kano wants to know whether demand for a product is growing, and the Kano Chamber of Commerce helps her find the answer. A chamber is broader than a trade association because it brings together traders, manufacturers and service providers from many sectors.

Its objectives are to promote trade and industry, encourage enterprise and safeguard the business community. Its functions include conducting research and publishing statistics, providing arbitration and training, and representing business views to government. The Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry does similar work for its members and the wider public.
bullets: Objective: promote trade, enterprise and the interests of business.
Function: research, statistics, arbitration, training and matchmaking for members.
Function: represent the business community to government and the public.
content.takeaway: Chambers promote trade and industry and speak for business as a whole.

check.question: Which activity is mainly a function of a chamber of commerce?
options: Arbitration, research and representing business to government
Setting garri prices in one market
check.why: Chambers provide cross-trade services and speak for business as a whole.

content.heading: Forms of business combination
paragraphs: Two operating garri mills in the same town decide to join as one company. That is a horizontal combination because the firms do the same work at the same stage. A cement maker who buys a quarry that supplies its raw material is a vertical combination because the firms work at different stages of one chain.

A conglomerate joins unrelated businesses, such as a food company that also owns a transport firm, under one owner. A cartel is different because there is no merger at all: rival firms agree to fix prices or output. The test is therefore simple: same stage means horizontal, different stages means vertical, unrelated trades means conglomerate, and agreement without ownership means cartel.
bullets: Horizontal: firms at the same stage merge, such as two garri mills.
Vertical: firms at different stages join, such as a mill and its quarry.
Conglomerate: unrelated firms join under one owner for wider risk.
Cartel: rivals agree on price or output without becoming one firm.
content.takeaway: Same stage is horizontal, different stages vertical, unrelated conglomerate, agreement cartel.

check.question: A firm buys its raw material supplier. Which form is this?
check.why: Different stages of one chain joined by ownership means a vertical combination.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Name the stage first, then the link. Same stage points to a horizontal merger and different stages to a vertical one, while a cartel has no merger at all and a conglomerate joins unrelated trades.

content.problem: Two poultry feed makers at the same stage merge into one company. Which form of business combination is this, and why?

steps.reason: Both firms make feed at the same stage of the chain.
steps.result: They are direct rivals, so the link is horizontal.

steps.reason: The firms join as one company, so ownership is shared.
steps.result: It is a true business combination, not a cartel agreement.

steps.reason: No different-stage supply link and no unrelated trade is involved.
steps.result: The answer is a horizontal merger, not vertical, conglomerate or cartel.

content.question: A cement company buys the limestone quarry that supplies it. Which form of business combination is this, and why?
hints: Look at the stages of production before you decide.
The cement maker and the quarry work at different stages.
The link is through ownership, so it is not a cartel.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why traders organise instead of competing alone
paragraphs: One trader alone bears the full cost of a problem, such as a sudden rise in the price of raw garri. The trader must pay for the information, travel to officials and wait for a reply while still serving customers. An association spreads that cost across many members, so research, representation and legal advice become affordable for each person.

It also solves a timing problem that a single trader cannot solve. Price information gathered in one market can be shared in another market within days, so members can buy and stock with better knowledge. Quality rules agreed by the association are easier to enforce when members inspect each other and sanction those who cheat on weight or grading.

The gain is not automatic, because members can free ride on the work of others without contributing fees. Associations therefore use registers, dues and penalties to keep cooperation stable and to exclude those who refuse to pay. That discipline is why a strong association can speak credibly while a loose mailing list cannot.
bullets: Joint action spreads the cost of information and representation.
Shared intelligence lets members price and stock with better knowledge.
Dues and sanctions protect the association against free riding.
A united voice raises bargaining power with suppliers and officials.

content.heading: Go deeper: How a chamber differs from a trade association
paragraphs: A trade association is organised around one commodity or trade, such as cocoa farming or garri selling. Its members sell or make the same kind of good and face the same risks, such as disease in cocoa or a sudden glut of garri. A chamber is organised around a place and its whole business community, so its membership must cut across many trades at once.

That difference in scope changes what each body can do. A trade association can fix a grading rule for its commodity, run a specialised training programme and set a minimum price for its members. A chamber must serve many trades at once, so it focuses on wider needs such as market research, trade fairs, arbitration and business information for any firm in the area.

Membership follows the same logic. A trade association is open only to those in the trade, while a chamber admits traders, manufacturers, bankers and professionals from many sectors. In Nigeria, the Lagos, Kano and Ogun chambers have used that wider base to advise government on taxes, power and trade policy in ways a single trade could not, because they speak for employment and investment as a whole.
bullets: Trade association: one commodity, narrow membership, technical rules.
Chamber: many sectors, place-based membership, general business services.
Chambers act for the whole business community, not one trade.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cartels, mergers and why the law cares
paragraphs: A cartel looks like a merger but behaves differently, because the firms remain separate owners. Each member has an incentive to cheat by secretly selling more than its agreed share while hoping others restrain output. That temptation is why cartels often collapse without a court or inspector to punish cheating, and why the law treats price fixing between rivals with suspicion.

A merger removes that temptation by making the firms one owner, which can save costs through a larger warehouse, one logistics team or joint research. A horizontal merger can also cut competition, because two rivals become one seller who can raise prices. Business combination law therefore weighs efficiency against the loss of rivalry, and asks whether consumers still have a choice.

Nigerian practice reflects that balance in a practical way. Trade associations and chambers may publish prices and standards for their members, but an agreement that fixes prices across rivals draws legal concern. The exam test is not whether cooperation is good or bad, but whether ownership has merged or the agreement merely coordinates prices, which is what separates a cartel from a true combination.
bullets: Cartels are fragile because cheating pays while the firm stays separate.
Mergers save costs but can reduce competition and raise prices.
The law asks whether rivals merged or merely agreed to coordinate.
Ownership is the test that separates a cartel from a merger.

lessons.title: Stock Exchange
lessons.objective: State the importance and functions of the Stock Exchange, identify the different securities traded on the Stock Exchange, analyse the procedure of transactions and speculations on the Stock Exchange, and appraise the advantages and operating regulations of the market.

content.heading: Stock exchange
paragraphs: Companies need large capital and savers need a safe place to invest. The Nigerian Exchange Group provides that meeting place. This lesson explains its functions, the securities it trades and how transactions settle.

content.heading: Why the stock exchange exists
paragraphs: A factory in Kaduna needs new machinery that costs far more than its profit can provide. A teacher in Enugu has savings that could help, but she has never met the factory owner. The Nigerian Exchange Group, NGX, brings such savers and such firms together in one regulated marketplace.

Its importance is that it channels savings into productive investment while giving savers a chance to sell what they own. Its core functions are to raise long term capital for companies, provide a place where investors can buy and sell securities, and discover prices through open trading.
bullets: Importance: channels savings into investment and offers investors a ready market to sell.
Function: raises long term capital for companies through new issues.
Function: provides price discovery, liquidity and transparent trading under NGX rules.
content.takeaway: The exchange links savers to firms and lets investors trade easily.

check.question: Which function makes the stock exchange important to a new company?
options: Raising long term capital from the public
Fixing the price of the company's products
Lending the company short term emergency cash
check.why: The exchange channels public savings to the firm as long term capital.

content.heading: Securities and how a deal happens
paragraphs: The exchange trades several securities, and each is a different promise. Ordinary stocks and shares give ownership and a share of profit, preference shares give a fixed dividend before ordinary shares, bonds are loans to government or large firms, and debentures are asset-backed loans that offer fixed interest with security.

An investor does not walk onto the floor. She opens an account with a licensed stockbroker, who places her order on the NGX platform, matches it with another order and arranges settlement. Speculation is buying in the hope that the price will rise, unlike investing which seeks income and growth over time.
bullets: Shares are ownership; bonds and debentures are loans with interest.
A stockbroker places the order, matches it and arranges settlement.
Speculation seeks a price rise; investing seeks income and growth.
content.takeaway: Shares own the firm, bonds lend to it, brokers trade it.

check.question: Which security gives the holder a loan with fixed interest?
check.why: Bonds are loans to government or firms that pay fixed interest.

content.heading: Listing, the Second-Tier and the rules
paragraphs: A public limited company lists when it offers shares on the exchange and meets NGX rules on disclosure, audited accounts and governance. Smaller and growing firms use the Second-Tier, now the Growth Board, where the requirements are lighter but the securities are less liquid.

Listing gives wide capital, publicity and a ready market to sell shares, but it also brings strict reporting and trading discipline. Operating regulations cover who may trade, how prices are formed, how misconduct is punished and how investors are protected, so that the market remains fair.
bullets: Listing needs disclosure, audited accounts and proper governance.
Second-Tier or Growth Board suits smaller firms with lighter rules.
Advantages include wide capital and liquidity; rules protect investors.
content.takeaway: Listing sells shares to the public under rules that protect investors.

check.question: Which statement best describes the Second-Tier market?
options: It is only for government securities
It serves smaller and growing companies with lighter listing rules
It allows firms to avoid all disclosure
check.why: The Second-Tier, now the Growth Board, admits smaller firms on lighter requirements.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Sort the security by what the holder gets. Ownership points to shares, a loan with interest points to bonds or debentures, and a short term price aim points to speculation rather than investing.

content.problem: An investor buys shares through a stockbroker and sells them later at a higher price. Classify the motive and name the steps.

steps.reason: The investor buys and later sells through a licensed stockbroker.
steps.result: The deal passes through the NGX platform to settlement.

steps.reason: The gain comes from a higher resale price, not from dividends.
steps.result: The motive is speculation for a capital gain.

steps.reason: Investing seeks steady income and long term growth of the firm.
steps.result: Selling quickly for a price rise shows speculation, not investing.

content.question: A teacher buys government bonds for steady interest and holds them for years. Is this speculation or investment, and why?
hints: Look at the return she expects from the bonds.
Steady interest for years is income, not a price rise.
Holding for years seeks safety and income, not quick resale.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why shares, bonds and debentures are different promises
paragraphs: An ordinary shareholder owns part of a company and shares its profit after costs, wages and lenders are paid. The return comes as dividends when profits allow, and the share price can rise or fall with the fortunes of the firm. A shareholder also votes at meetings, so ownership carries control as well as risk.

A bondholder is a lender, not an owner, and receives fixed interest whether profits rise or fall. The loan is repaid at maturity, and bondholders are paid before shareholders when a firm fails. Preference shares sit between the two, because they take a fixed dividend before ordinary shares but normally do not vote as freely as ordinary shareholders.

Debentures add security to that lending promise. A debenture is backed by the assets of the firm, so the lender can claim a specific asset if the firm defaults, while an unsecured bond has no such claim. That asset backing lowers risk for the lender and usually lowers the interest rate, which is why the exam treats debentures as secured loans rather than ownership.
bullets: Shares own the firm; bonds and debentures lend to it.
Preference shares rank before ordinary shares for income.
Debentures are secured by assets; bonds may be unsecured.

content.heading: Go deeper: From order to settlement
paragraphs: A deal on the Nigerian Exchange Group begins with an instruction, not with cash in hand. The investor tells a licensed stockbroker how many securities to buy or sell, the broker checks the account and places the order on the exchange platform, where it meets an opposite order. That matching is what discovers the price at any moment.

Once matched, the trade is cleared and settled through central systems. The buyer pays and the seller delivers the security, with records held electronically rather than as paper certificates. The broker, the exchange and the clearing house each keep a record, so that neither side can deny the bargain and the market stays transparent.

Market tiers organise that flow by size and risk. The Main Board carries larger listed companies with close scrutiny, while the Growth Board, formerly called the Second-Tier, carries smaller firms with lighter requirements and thinner trading. A speculator trades inside that same chain but with a different aim, because the price rise is expected within a short period rather than from long term dividends.
bullets: Stockbroker places the order; the platform matches opposite orders.
Clearing and settlement transfer money and securities safely.
Tiers separate large firms from smaller, thinner trades.

content.heading: Go deeper: Listing and the Second-Tier choice
paragraphs: Listing is a decision to sell shares to the public under NGX supervision. The firm must publish a prospectus, produce audited accounts, disclose major risks and adopt governance that protects outside shareholders. Those costs buy the firm access to wide capital, greater publicity and a market where investors can sell quickly, but they also bind the firm to regular reporting for as long as it stays listed.

The Second-Tier idea recognises that those full costs would exclude smaller firms. By placing them on the Growth Board with lighter capital and reporting requirements, the exchange lets a growing company raise money earlier than the Main Board would allow. The trade-off is liquidity, because fewer investors follow a small listing, so prices move more sharply and selling can be slower.

Operating regulations hold the two boards together. They decide who may act as a broker, how trading is suspended for misconduct, how insider dealing is punished and how price limits guard against panic. Those rules explain why a listed firm accepts discipline, because without disclosure, audit and fair trading the market could not channel savings to firms with confidence.
bullets: Listing trades higher reporting costs for wider capital.
Second-Tier or Growth Board lowers entry costs for smaller firms.
Regulations on disclosure and conduct sustain investor confidence.

lessons.title: Elements of Business Management
lessons.objective: Appraise the functions of management, analyse the principles of management, identify organisational structures, assess the functional areas of business, and examine the business resources.

content.heading: Elements of business management
paragraphs: Ngozi runs a provisions shop in Lagos and a bakery in Surulere. Both businesses make money, yet stock runs out and staff quarrel. The missing ingredient is management: planning, organising and controlling resources so results last.

content.heading: The work of managers: seven functions
paragraphs: Ngozi must decide what to stock for the month, arrange the shelves and hire an assistant. A manager in Konga's delivery hub does the same at larger scale. These duties are the functions of management, the process that turns resources into results.

Planning sets goals and chooses courses of action. Organising arranges resources, staffing recruits and trains, and coordinating aligns every unit. Motivating energises staff, communicating shares information, and controlling compares results with the plan and corrects the gaps.
bullets: Planning sets the goals; organising arranges resources to reach them.
Staffing recruits and trains; coordinating aligns units; motivating gives energy.
Communicating shares information; controlling compares results with the plan.
Each function feeds the next: a plan that is not controlled is only a wish.
content.takeaway: Planning, organising, staffing, coordinating, motivating, communicating and controlling form one continuous management cycle.

check.question: A supermarket manager compares this month's sales with the target and moves a cashier to the busiest till. Which function of management is she performing?
check.why: Controlling compares actual results with the plan and corrects the gaps.

content.heading: Principles and structures: how authority is arranged
paragraphs: Ngozi's two assistants both receive orders from her and from her wholesaler. When instructions clash, the junior cannot obey both. Unity of command exists to prevent that clash: each worker takes orders from one boss.

Span of control counts how many people one manager supervises well. Delegation of authority passes the right to decide downwards, but accountability stays with the delegating manager. Span counts people while unity names the boss.

A line structure runs in one vertical chain, as in Ngozi's shop. Line and staff adds specialists who advise but do not command, functional gives specialists charge of their own units, matrix gives each worker two bosses, and committee decides as a group.
bullets: Unity of command: one worker, one boss, so instructions never clash.
Span of control counts how many one manager supervises; delegation passes authority but not accountability.
Line, line and staff, functional, matrix and committee are five organisational structures.
content.takeaway: Each worker answers to one boss; the span stops any manager being overstretched.

check.question: A worker takes orders from two supervisors and is confused. Which principle is broken?
check.why: Unity of command requires one boss per worker, so two bosses mean conflicting instructions.

content.heading: Where work happens: functional areas and resources
paragraphs: A pure-water factory in Ikeja produces, a Konga seller markets, a bank lends and a supermarket recruits. These are the functional areas of a business: production makes goods, marketing sells them, finance funds them and personnel recruits and trains the people.

Every area combines five business resources: man (human effort), money, materials, machines, and opportunity with goodwill. Managers must deploy all five because a shortage in any one of them stalls the whole business.
Opportunity is the market gap worth filling, while goodwill is the reputation that brings customers back. Ngozi's bakery succeeds on a gap for evening bread and loyal customers who trust her loaves.
bullets: Production creates, marketing sells, finance funds, personnel staffs the business.
Man, money, materials and machines are worked resources every business combines.
Opportunity is the gap worth filling; goodwill is the reputation that returns customers.
content.takeaway: Production, marketing, finance and personnel deploy man, money, materials, machines, opportunity and goodwill.

check.question: A firm turns cassava into garri and sells it in Lagos. Which functional area does the turning belong to?
check.why: Production transforms materials into goods; marketing would sell them.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question names a duty, choose a function of management; when it names a reporting relationship, choose a principle or a structure. Span of control is about numbers, while unity of command is about the single boss.

content.problem: A wholesaler employs 15 salesmen reporting directly to the owner. Two receive conflicting instructions from the owner and the marketing manager. Which principle is broken, and which function repairs it? A. Unity of command; organising B. Span of control; staffing C. Delegation; controlling D. Division of work; planning

steps.reason: Two bosses create conflicting orders, the symptom unity of command forbids.
steps.result: Unity of command is broken; option A names it.

steps.reason: Fifteen direct reports exceed a workable span of control for one manager.
steps.result: Repair means organising a narrower structure, confirming A.

steps.reason: Staffing would concern recruitment; controlling compares results, and planning sets goals.
steps.result: The answer is A: unity of command, organising.

content.question: A new supermarket in Abuja opens with no written goals, 20 staff reporting to one manager and a marketing manager who orders them around. Name one function of management, one principle and one structure that have failed, and suggest a fix for each.
hints: No written goals means planning has failed; set targets for sales and stock first.
Twenty staff under one manager breaks span of control; add supervisors to narrow the span.
Two bosses break unity of command; adopt line and staff, where the marketing manager advises rather than commands.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why accountability cannot be delegated
paragraphs: Authority is the right to decide and to give orders. Responsibility is the duty to carry out assigned work. Accountability is owning the outcome, good or bad, and it is the one element that cannot be delegated.

A branch manager in Lagos can delegate a loan approval to a senior officer. The officer gains authority and responsibility for that decision. If the loan fails, the branch manager still answers to the bank for it.

That split explains two common delegation mistakes. A manager who hands over paperwork but keeps every decision has not delegated at all. A manager who delegates and then disowns a failure has broken accountability, because the result still belongs to the delegator.

Span of control decides how far delegation can go. One manager who delegates to fifteen people soon becomes a bottleneck, and accountability grows hard to trace. A narrow span keeps both the orders and the answers clear.
bullets: Authority and responsibility move downwards; accountability stays put.
Delegation without decisions is paperwork, not delegation.
Accountability is the test: the delegator answers when the work fails.
A narrow span keeps orders and answers clear.

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing a structure as a business grows
paragraphs: A bakery with three workers runs as a line: the owner decides, orders travel down, and answers travel up. When a Lagos supermarket grows to fifty staff, that single chain chokes. Line and staff adds a finance officer and a personnel adviser, who supply expertise but still report to line managers.

A functional structure goes further. Each specialist commands the unit: production answers to the production head, finance to the finance head, and marketing to the marketing head. The cost is duplication, because each unit keeps its own records and staff.

A matrix structure handles projects by giving each worker two bosses, one from the functional unit and one from the project. A firm building a road needs engineers and site teams to work together for the life of the project. The benefit is flexibility; the price is confusion, because unity of command is deliberately broken.

A committee structure places decisions in a group, as in a school governing board or a traders' association. It suits broad agreement but moves slowly. The examination test is who decides: line decides, staff advises, functional commands within a unit, matrix shares, and committee votes.
bullets: Line suits small firms; functional suits many departments.
Matrix suits projects; committee suits broad agreement.
Staff advise but do not command: that is the line and staff test.

content.heading: Go deeper: Opportunity and goodwill as quiet resources
paragraphs: Opportunity is a market gap that can be filled profitably. A Lagos trader who notices that evening bread is scarce has found an opportunity, but she must test it: how many buyers, at what price, and against which rivals? An opportunity that fails the test is only an idea.

Goodwill is the reputation that brings customers back. It is built by consistent quality, honest measures and fair treatment, but it is lost just as quickly by late delivery or adulterated goods, and a shop with loyal customers sells for more than its shelves and stock. When the shop changes hands, the buyer pays for that trust, not just for the shelves.

The two resources explain the five-resource list. Man, money, materials and machines are bought and counted, while opportunity and goodwill are earned and lost. A business that owns the first four but misses the last two produces goods that nobody quite wants to buy.
bullets: Opportunity is tested by buyers, price and rivals, not by hope.
Goodwill is earned by quality and honesty and lost by service failures.
A shop with goodwill sells for more than its stock and shelves.
The first four resources are bought; the last two are earned and lost.

lessons.title: Elements of Marketing
lessons.objective: Highlight the importance and functions of marketing, discuss the marketing concept, assess the elements of marketing mix, explain market segmentation, examine public relations and customer service, and explain e-marketing.

content.heading: Elements of marketing
paragraphs: A trader on Konga lists phone chargers an hour after a rival posts the same charger cheaper. Buyers still order from her. Marketing finds buyers, satisfies them and keeps them; that work decides who stays in business.

content.heading: Why marketing matters: functions and the marketing concept
paragraphs: A Lagos boutique that imports aso-ebi and rents an expensive shop can still collapse. Marketing is the set of activities that find buyers, tell them about the offer, deliver value and keep them buying. Its work raises sales, widens choice and earns revenue for the business.

The marketing concept has three parts. Consumer orientation starts from buyer needs rather than from the factory. Customer satisfaction gives buyers value beyond their expectations, and integrated marketing makes every department serve the same customer goal.

On Konga, a seller who keeps delivery promises is promoted more widely. One department's promise is another department's cost, so integrated marketing coordinates delivery, pricing and promotion to the same customer goal.
bullets: Importance: marketing finds buyers, informs them and keeps them buying.
Consumer orientation starts from buyer needs; satisfaction keeps them.
Integrated marketing coordinates every department to one customer goal.
