content.takeaway: Marketing starts from the customer in order to satisfy and retain that customer.

check.question: A soap maker redesigns its bar after buyers complain of dry skin. Which part of the marketing concept is it applying?
check.why: Consumer orientation starts from buyer needs, so the redesign follows buyer feedback.

content.heading: The marketing mix and market segmentation
paragraphs: Chidi sews shoes in Surulere and sells through a shop and Instagram. His product is the shoe itself. His price is what buyers pay, his place is the shop and delivery network where they can buy, and his promotion is the Instagram photographs and offers that tell buyers he exists.

The market is too large to serve equally, so Chidi segments it into buyers who value cheap sandals and buyers who value custom-made shoes. Segmentation divides a market into groups with similar needs or buying behaviour, using place, age and income, lifestyle or loyalty as tests.
bullets: Product is the offer, price is what buyers pay, place is where they buy, promotion tells buyers.
Segmentation groups buyers by geography, age and income, lifestyle or loyalty.
A mix built for one segment fails when it is served to another.
content.takeaway: Product, price, place and promotion must answer the needs of one chosen segment.

check.question: Jumia delivers in Lagos within a day but takes a week to a northern city. Which element of the marketing mix differs between the two markets?
check.why: Place means where and how buyers obtain the good; delivery reach is place.

content.heading: Reputation and reach: public relations, service and e-marketing
paragraphs: When a Konga seller's parcel arrives damaged, she replaces it and apologises. That after-sales help is customer service, the work that keeps buyers after the sale. Public relations is different: it builds the firm's reputation with the public, the media and the community, without directly selling.

E-marketing moves both activities online. Jumia and Konga take orders, payments and complaints through apps and websites, and hotels take bookings through travel portals. The gain is reach and lower cost; the risks are fraud, delivery failure and the loss of the face-to-face check.
bullets: Public relations builds reputation with publics; it does not sell directly.
Customer service keeps buyers after the sale through support and redress.
E-marketing sells and serves through websites, apps, social media and email.
content.takeaway: Reputation, service and online selling win the buyer and keep the buyer.

check.question: A bank refunds a customer whose transfer failed and apologises for the delay. Which activity is it performing?
check.why: Customer service handles after-sales complaints and redress; advertising would promote an offer.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Reputation questions point to public relations, after-sales questions point to customer service, and where-buyers-buy questions point to place. When the sale happens online, e-marketing is the best choice of all.

content.problem: A firm sells premium shoes through one Lagos mall shop only, with no online store. A rival sells similar shoes on Jumia, in its own shops and on Instagram. (a) Name two elements of the marketing mix that differ. (b) How should segmentation guide the firm's response?

steps.reason: Place is where buyers buy; one shop versus shops plus online is a place gap.
Promotion is how buyers are told; Instagram and Jumia listings have no mall-shop equivalent.
Premium buyers accept a single location, while deal-seekers need online discounts and delivery.
steps.result: Serve the mall segment for experience and the Jumia segment for price and speed.

content.question: A Kano textiles trader starts on WhatsApp, takes transfers and delivers by rider. Name one marketing-mix element and one e-marketing advantage and one trust problem she must solve.
hints: WhatsApp selling is place (online channel) and the delivery is also place.
Reach and lower cost are advantages; trust and delivery failure are problems.
She needs ratings, honest photographs and a clear refund promise to build trust.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the four Ps must work as one mix
paragraphs: Changing one P changes the meaning of the others. A premium price signals quality, but only when the product, the shop and the promotion support that signal. A N50,000 shoe sold from a tarpaulin stall, with no advertising, asks buyers to believe a story the other Ps do not tell.

Place and promotion must agree as well. A seller who advertises widely but delivers late has bought attention and spent trust. Konga and Jumia learned this by making delivery promises that feed the listings that promote them, instead of letting the two Ps drift apart.

Product decisions set the same chain in motion, because a shoe made for one buyer cannot be priced for another. A shoe made for schoolchildren in Kano cannot be priced for bankers in Ikoyi, nor distributed only through boutiques. Each P therefore limits the choices left for the others, and the mix is sound only when all four pull together.
bullets: Price signals quality only when product, place and promotion support it.
Advertising without delivery spends trust while buying attention.
A P that contradicts the others wastes what the others have built.
If promotion promises what place cannot deliver, buyers stop believing either.

content.heading: Go deeper: Segmentation bases and the cost of serving everyone
paragraphs: Segmentation is a decision about whom to serve first. A geographically divided market, like Lagos against rural northern towns, forces different delivery promises and different prices. Serving both from one warehouse is possible, but it is rarely the cheapest route.

Demographic tests divide by age and income, while psychographic tests divide by lifestyle and values. Behavioural tests divide by loyalty and buying rate. A firm that knows which test matters can spend its budget on the segment that will actually buy.

The cost of serving everyone is a thin mix. A shop that sells budget sandals and custom shoes from one counter must price, stock and promote for neither. Under-segmentation is therefore an error: the mix is spread so thin that no segment feels served.

Konga's Express badge shows behavioural segmentation in practice. Buyers who pay for speed and reliability receive the fastest delivery, while slower buyers pay less and wait. The badge is a promise the logistics must keep, because a broken promise loses the segment that chose it.
bullets: Geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural are four segmentation tests.
Under-segmentation spreads the mix until no segment feels served.
A segment is defined by shared needs, not by location alone.

content.heading: Go deeper: E-marketing, trust and customer service online
paragraphs: E-marketing replaces the shop counter with a screen. Jumia and Konga take orders, payments and complaints through apps and websites, and hotels take bookings through travel portals. That reach is the first advantage, because a trader in Lagos can sell to a buyer in Jos without renting space there.

The second advantage is cost. A shop charges rent, power and staff, while a listing charges a smaller commission. But e-marketing removes the face-to-face check, so buyers need trust: ratings, return windows and payment protection stand in for the handshake.

Trust failures show up as public relations problems. A delayed parcel that is never explained becomes a review, a screenshot and a lost segment. Customer service online is therefore reactive: refunds and apologies must arrive before the rating hardens.

Pay-on-delivery answers the trust gap by moving the risk to the seller. It works in Lagos, but it also invites fake orders and cash handling. E-marketing is therefore not simply cheaper selling; it is a different balance of reach, cost, trust and redress.
bullets: E-marketing trades rent and staff for commission, reach and trust risk.
Ratings, return windows and payment protection replace the handshake.
An unexplained delay becomes a review and a lost segment.

lessons.title: Legal Aspects of Business
lessons.objective: Analyse the elements and validity of a simple contract; examine Agency, Sale of Goods Act and Hire Purchase Act; assess the rights and obligations of employers and employees; distinguish between patents, trademarks and copyrights; identify the functions of consumerism; and assess the relevance of regulatory agencies and acts in the provision of safe goods and drugs.

content.heading: Legal aspects of business
paragraphs: A trader in Onitsha promises land to a buyer but refuses delivery. Only a valid contract, agency rules, employment law and consumer law explain who must perform and who can sue.

content.heading: What makes a contract valid
paragraphs: Uche offers to sell his phone for ₦80,000. Bola accepts at once, and Uche later claims he was only joking.

An offer is a definite promise meant to be accepted, and acceptance must match it exactly without new conditions. Consideration is the price of the promise: each side must give money, goods or a promise in return, so a gift is not a contract.

Both parties must have capacity, meaning legal power to contract, so minors and persons of unsound mind need protection. The purpose must also be lawful; a promise to smuggle goods cannot be enforced even if offer, acceptance and consideration exist.
bullets: Offer must be clear and intended for acceptance
Acceptance must be unqualified and communicated to the offeror
Consideration is something of value given by each side
Capacity and lawful purpose make the agreement enforceable
content.takeaway: A valid contract requires offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity and lawful purpose.

check.question: Which agreement is a valid simple contract?
options: Uche promises a free gift expecting no return
Bola promises to pay ₦50,000 for Uche's phone and Uche accepts
A minor promises to buy a phone without any support
Musa promises to pay for smuggled phones
check.why: Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity and lawful purpose are all present only in B.

content.heading: Agency, sale, hire purchase and work
paragraphs: A trader in Kano sends a boy to buy goods, but the supplier asks who pays if the trader refuses them. Agency law decides whether the agent binds the principal who appointed the agent.

The Sale of Goods Act protects the buyer with good title, fitness for purpose and merchantable quality. Hire purchase differs because ownership passes only after the last instalment, so the hirer holds goods as bailee, not owner.

Employment binds the employer to pay wages, provide safety and respect notice, and the employee to work honestly and keep secrets. Remember the pair: a buyer owns at once, but a hirer owns only after full payment.
bullets: An agent acts for the principal and can bind the principal
Sale of goods gives the buyer title, fitness and quality
Hire purchase gives possession now and ownership only at the end
Employers pay and protect; employees serve honestly and keep secrets
content.takeaway: Agency links agent and principal; sale gives title, hire purchase delays it.

check.question: A shopper takes a fridge on hire purchase, to own it after twelve instalments. What is her position before payment ends?
options: She is the owner at once
She is a bailee with an option to own
She is an agent for the shop
She has no obligation to pay
check.why: Ownership passes only after the last instalment, so she is a bailee until then.

content.heading: Registration, intellectual property and consumer protection
paragraphs: A trader registers a bakery name with the Corporate Affairs Commission, then copies another maker's logo. Registration protects the trader's identity, but copying the logo breaks trademark law.

A patent protects an invention, a trademark protects a sign such as a name or logo, and copyright protects a work such as a book or song. The test is what is protected: invention, sign, or expression, and only the patent needs novelty.

Consumer law guards the buyer. The Standards Organisation of Nigeria sets product standards, NAFDAC controls food and drugs, the Consumer Protection Commission handles complaints, and the Trade Descriptions Act bans false claims. Customs stops smuggled goods and NDLEA fights drug trafficking.
bullets: Business registration gives the firm a legal identity for contracts
Patent, trademark and copyright protect invention, sign and expression
Consumer agencies ensure safe, honestly described goods
SON, NAFDAC and the Consumer Protection Commission guard food, drugs and complaints
content.takeaway: Register the business, protect the invention, sign or work, and serve safe goods.

check.question: A singer records a new song. Which protection stops others copying the recording as their own work?
check.why: Copyright protects expression such as a book or song; patents protect inventions and trademarks protect signs.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question names a promise, test the five validity elements before you decide. Gift, incapacity or illegality defeats the claim, and a hirer becomes a buyer only after the last payment.

content.problem: Ade offers Bala ₦30,000 for his bicycle. Bala accepts. Is there a valid contract? A. Yes B. No, because oral C. Yes, because written D. No, because low value

steps.reason: A definite promise meant for acceptance is the first element.
Bala accepted exactly, and ₦30,000 is something of value in return.
steps.result: Acceptance and consideration are both present.

steps.reason: Both adults can contract and the purpose is lawful trading.
steps.result: Answer is A: a valid contract exists.

content.question: Tunde signs a one-year agreement to supply yam to a college. Name the elements that make it a contract.
hints: Look for the offer and the exact acceptance.
Identify what each side gives in return.
Check that both can contract and the purpose is lawful.

content.heading: Go deeper: Offer, consideration and capacity in practice
paragraphs: A shop display with a price tag is usually an invitation to treat, not an offer. The customer invites the shop to accept, so the shop may refuse the sale until goods are tendered at the till. A newspaper advertisement behaves the same way, while an offer sent to a named buyer is different because it can be accepted.

Consideration must move from the promisee, meaning the person who wants the promise enforced must also give value. A past act done before the promise usually fails, and a moral duty alone is not enough, because the law requires a bargain. Consideration can be small, yet it must be real, not a peppercorn in a mockery.

Capacity protects those who cannot protect themselves. A minor can buy necessaries such as food and shelter, but an expensive phone may be voidable, meaning an adult can later avoid it. A person who is intoxicated or of unsound mind is protected when the other side knows of the problem.
bullets: Invitation to treat is not an offer until acceptance at the counter
Consideration must be a real bargain moving from the promisee
Minors are bound only for necessaries and may avoid other bargains
Intoxication or unsoundness protects only when the other side knows

content.heading: Go deeper: Agency, sale and hire purchase traps
paragraphs: An agent can bind a principal only when acting within the authority given. Express authority is stated in words or writing, while implied authority covers acts needed for the job, such as a shop assistant accepting payment. An agent who exceeds authority may be personally liable, because the principal is not bound.

The Sale of Goods Act mainly fills gaps when parties say little. If goods are described, they must match the description; if the buyer examines goods, hidden faults still matter; and if time is fixed, the court treats it strictly. These implied terms help buyers where bargaining power is weak.

Hire purchase protects the dealer more than an ordinary sale would suggest. The hirer has possession, must keep the goods well and must not sell or pledge them before ownership passes. Default lets the owner repossess under the agreement, but wrongful repossession can itself breach the Hire Purchase Act.
bullets: Express and implied authority define what an agent may do
Sale terms fill gaps on description, fitness and quality
Hirer is a bailee and must keep and not dispose of goods
Ownership in hire purchase waits for the last instalment

content.heading: Go deeper: Intellectual property, agencies and consumer redress
paragraphs: The Corporate Affairs Commission registers companies and business names, giving a legal identity that can own property and sue. Registration does not itself grant a trademark, so a registered business name can still infringe another logo. A patent application needs a new invention, while a trademark can last for years if it remains in use.

Consumer protection works through several roles that must not be confused. The Standards Organisation of Nigeria sets and enforces product standards, NAFDAC registers food, drugs and cosmetics, and the Consumer Protection Commission receives complaints and educates buyers. The Trade Descriptions Act punishes false statements about size, origin or content, and Customs intercepts smuggled or substandard imports.

Complaints usually move from seller to agency to court, but buyers should keep receipts, samples and photographs. The NDLEA, which fights drug trafficking and abuse, is not a product regulator for soap or food, so it should not be confused with NAFDAC. Clear labels and accurate descriptions prevent most disputes before they reach an agency.
bullets: Registration gives identity but not rights in a name or mark
Patents require novelty; marks require use; works require originality
Agencies have separate roles for standards, products and complaints
Keep evidence so a failed product can be proved quickly

lessons.title: Commodity Exchange
lessons.objective: Explain the meaning of commodity exchange, highlight types of tradable commodity, list the requirements for trading, discuss methods of trading, enumerate the benefits of commodity exchange, and analyse the constraints to commodity trading.

content.heading: Commodity exchange
paragraphs: A farmer in Jos grows maize but has no buyer until harvest. A commodity exchange brings farmers, buyers and warehouses together, so standard goods trade quickly at a public price.

content.heading: What a commodity exchange is
paragraphs: A maize farmer sells to anyone, yet every buyer worries about moisture and weight. The exchange solves this by trading only standard grades, so the contract promises grade, not a particular farmer's heap.

Tradable commodities are organised by source and include agricultural produce such as maize, cocoa, palm oil and cotton. Solid minerals include tin, gold and gypsum, while oil and gas include crude oil and natural gas. Each type needs different handling and storage.

The exchange is a central market that links producers, dealers and buyers through standard contracts. Unlike a village market, it guarantees delivery of the grade promised, so wheat from any member can settle the trade.
bullets: Exchange trades standard grades, not named sellers
Agricultural produce, solid minerals and oil and gas are tradable
Contracts promise grade and quantity for settlement
Central market links producers, dealers and buyers
content.takeaway: A commodity exchange trades standard grades through central contracts.

check.question: Which is a tradable commodity on an exchange?
options: A single farmer's ungraded heap of maize
Cassava chips to an agreed grade
check.why: The exchange trades standard grades, so cassava chips to an agreed grade fit, while the others do not.

content.heading: Conditions and ways of trading
paragraphs: No trade can start until goods are graded and standardised. The grade fixes moisture, size or purity, so a buyer and seller mean the same quality. Standard contract sizes also let small lots combine into tradable units.

Warehouses store traded goods and issue receipts that assure buyers the goods exist. Clearing then settles payments and delivery between parties who may never meet. Without warehousing and clearing, the exchange would carry the risk of empty promises.

Two methods dominate. Open outcry uses traders shouting bids on a floor, while electronic trading matches orders by computer. Do not confuse outcry with electronic: the first is human and visible, the second is remote and recorded.
bullets: Grading and standardising fix quality and contract size
Warehousing assures buyers that goods exist and are stored
Clearing settles payment and delivery between strangers
Open outcry is floor shouting; electronic matching is computer based
content.takeaway: Grade, store and clear first; then outcry or electronic matching decides price.

check.question: Traders shout bids on a trading floor. Which method is that?
check.why: Shouting bids on a floor is open outcry; electronic trading matches orders by computer.

content.heading: Benefits and limits of exchange trading
paragraphs: The exchange benefits traders by widening markets and revealing prices to all. A farmer in Zaria can learn the Lagos price on the same day, and a miller can lock a price before harvest. Transparent pricing cuts the power of secret deals.

It also helps government and banks judge the economy. Price reports show scarcity early, while warehouse receipts can secure loans for stored goods. Farmers gain finance without a bank needing to visit the farm.

Constraints remain strong. Poor roads, weak warehousing and thin grades limit participation, while price falls can hurt those who locked high. In Nigeria, low volumes and mistrust of standard weights still thin the market.
bullets: Exchange widens markets and reveals a public price
Warehouse receipts secure bank loans more easily
Poor roads and weak warehousing exclude many farmers
Low volumes and mistrust thin the market
content.takeaway: Exchange shares prices and finance, but weak roads and trust limit it.

check.question: Which benefit does a warehouse receipt give a farmer?
options: It can secure a bank loan
check.why: Receipts assure lenders that stored goods exist, so they can secure credit.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Name the method before the benefit. Outcry is human shouting on a floor, electronic is computer matching, and warehousing does not decide price. When in doubt, ask whether the step fixes quality, stores goods or settles payment.

content.problem: A miller buys groundnut oil on the exchange and fears the seller will not deliver. Which requirement protects him? A. Grading B. Warehousing C. Open outcry D. Electronic matching

steps.reason: The miller fears non-delivery, not price debate on a floor.
steps.result: The risk is empty promises without goods.

steps.reason: Warehousing assures goods exist; clearing settles payment.
steps.result: Only warehousing covers the delivery fear.

steps.reason: Outcry and electronic matching set price but do not store goods.
steps.result: Answer is B: warehousing protects the miller.

content.question: A cocoa cooperative wants to sell Grade A beans next month. List what must happen before trading and name one benefit.
hints: Check grading, standard sizes and warehousing.
Add clearing to settle delivery.
Name price discovery or access to loans.

content.heading: Go deeper: How standard contracts settle trade
paragraphs: Standard contracts are fungible, meaning one unit can stand for another of the same grade. A buyer of Grade B cocoa does not care which farmer supplied it, because the grade already defines quality. This fungibility lets the exchange net off trades without moving goods each time.

Grading therefore matters more than the seller's name. Inspectors sample moisture, foreign matter and size, then assign the lot to a grade. If a load fails the grade, it cannot settle the contract, and the seller must find conforming goods or pay the price difference.

Cash settlement is the final step. Instead of moving goods, the loser pays the price difference to the winner, and the clearing house guarantees both sides. The guarantee lets strangers trade, because each trusts the house rather than the other party.

Worked practice shows the point: when a warehouse in Jos issues a receipt for Grade A maize, every later trade can rely on that receipt rather than on the farmer's word alone, and disputes over moisture disappear before they reach the clearing house.
bullets: Fungibility means grade, not the farmer, settles the duty
Inspection assigns a lot to a grade by sampling
Non-conforming lots cannot settle the contract
Cash settlement pays the price difference without moving goods

content.heading: Go deeper: Open outcry compared with electronic trading
paragraphs: Open outcry lets traders see and hear rivals, so a nod or shout can change price in seconds. The floor is noisy and local, but watching behaviour can signal urgency. A remote buyer without a seat cannot join, so the market stays small.

Electronic trading reverses those traits. Orders enter a system and match automatically, so a farmer's agent in Jos and a miller in Kano can trade without travel. The record is complete and auditable, which helps clearing, but the system needs power, data and rules against false orders.

The choice therefore affects access and trust. Floor trading builds personal reputation but excludes distant small sellers. Electronic trading widens access but creates new risks, such as mistaken clicks and system outages, so methods decide who can trade and how disputes are proved.

Examiners often set a trap here: electronic matching still needs grading and warehousing, because a computer cannot dry wet grain or build a warehouse in Jos, so the physical chain must be ready before any screen can trade.
bullets: Outcry is visible and fast but limited to those present
Electronic matching is remote, automatic and fully recorded
Floor markets rely on reputation; systems rely on audit trails
Both methods set price, yet neither stores or grades goods

content.heading: Go deeper: Why thin markets stay thin in Nigeria
paragraphs: A thin market has few trades, so prices jump on small news. With few sellers, one large lot can crash the price, and buyers wait rather than pay the high. The exchange then fails to attract more members, because the price looks unreliable.

Infrastructure decides the cure. All-weather roads cut transport loss, certified warehouses keep grain dry, and weights that buyers trust reduce disputes. Banks that accept warehouse receipts turn stored crops into credit, so farmers no longer sell at harvest for cash.

Oil and gas show a different constraint. Their grades are set by contracts and pipelines, not by village scales, so access depends on regulation and export channels. Solid minerals face smuggling and weak assay labs, which leave honest miners without a trusted grade.
The cure therefore starts outside the trading floor, with roads, power and trusted labs, before any new contract can add volume to the exchange in Nigeria and give honest sellers a fair price.
bullets: Few trades make prices jump and deter new members
Roads, warehouses and trusted weights thicken the market
Receipts turn stored goods into bank credit
Oil, gas and minerals need pipelines, regulation and assay labs

lessons.title: Business Environment and Social Responsibility
lessons.objective: Discuss the types of business environment, assess the role of social environment in the provision of safe products, and identify the different types of pollution and their implications on businesses.

content.heading: Business environment and social responsibility
paragraphs: A factory in Ogoni must obey the law, please customers and leave rivers clean. Its success depends on the legal, political, economic, social, cultural and technological environment around it.

content.heading: Six surroundings that shape business
paragraphs: A phone shop in Enugu faces import duties, a fall in income and new mobile money habits at once. No single shock explains its sales, because several surroundings press together.

The legal environment covers laws to obey, the political covers stability and policy, and the economic covers income and prices. The social covers habits and values, the cultural covers language and customs, and the technological covers tools and innovation. Each can help or hinder.

A rise in duties is political, a fall in wages is economic, and a new payment app is technological, yet all three reach the same till. A good manager watches each surrounding, because a change in one often drags the others.
bullets: Legal, political and economic surroundings set rules and demand
Social, cultural and technological surroundings set habits and tools
One change often drags others to the same till
Managers must watch all six at once
content.takeaway: Six surroundings of law, policy, income, habits, customs and tools shape business.

check.question: A new payment app spreads in a town. Which surrounding changed?
check.why: Tools and innovation belong to the technological environment.

content.heading: Safe products and service to society
paragraphs: A miller in Kano sells flour that makes buyers ill. A court may fine him, but reports of illness ruin trade faster. Safe products protect both health and the firm's name.

Philanthropy means voluntary giving such as schools or boreholes, while social responsibility is wider: the firm chooses to obey safety rules, treat workers fairly and consider neighbours. The first gives, the second governs how the firm operates daily.

Societal consideration adds the neighbours' views before the firm acts. It asks whether a new plant harms fishing or farming, and whether waste will be handled safely. A firm that listens early avoids protests and losses later.
bullets: Safe products meet standards and protect health
Philanthropy gives voluntarily; responsibility governs daily operation
Societal consideration weighs neighbour views before acting
Safe and considerate firms keep trust and trade
content.takeaway: Safe products, fair dealing and neighbour views build trust.

check.question: A company donates books to a school. That is mainly what?
check.why: Voluntary giving is philanthropy; safety and neighbour views are responsibility.

content.heading: Pollution that reaches the factory gate
paragraphs: A palm mill in Oyo pours waste into a stream, and fish die before the week ends. Water pollution costs the mill its buyers and the village its fish, so the firm pays twice.

Water pollution fouls rivers with oil or chemicals, air pollution fills air with smoke and gases, and land pollution salts soil with waste. Oil spills in the Niger Delta join all three, because crude spreads on water, chokes air and poisons farms.

For business, pollution means fines, lost fishing and farming, and a damaged name that deters buyers. Public health costs and clean-up bills fall on all, while honest firms lose customers to cheaper firms that dump freely.
bullets: Water, air and land pollution each harm a different medium
Oil spills in the Niger Delta join water, air and land
Pollution costs firms fines, sales and public trust
Clean-up and ill health fall on whole communities
content.takeaway: Water, air and land pollution, especially oil spills, damage business and health.

check.question: A firm dumps dye into a stream and fish die. Which pollution and cost fit?
options: Water pollution and public health costs
Land pollution and higher soil fertility
check.why: Dye in a stream is water pollution, and lost fish and ill health are public costs.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a question names a surrounding, ask what it governs. Duties and stability follow policy, income and prices follow economics, and tools follow technology. Philanthropy gives, while responsibility decides how the firm operates daily.

content.problem: A factory pays new import duties after a policy change. Which environment presses it most? A. Legal B. Political C. Social D. Cultural

steps.reason: Duties follow a government decision, not buyer habits.
Political environment covers stability and policy.
Legal is rules to obey, but the change came from policy.

content.question: A bakery in Ibadan wants to cut waste and keep neighbours happy. Name one safe-product step and one CSR step.
hints: Think of clean flour, water and labelled goods.
Add fair treatment of workers and nearby homes.
Avoid charity alone; describe daily operating choices.

content.heading: Go deeper: How the six surroundings interact
paragraphs: Surroundings rarely act alone. A new levy is political, but it raises prices, which is economic, and forces shops to adopt mobile payment, which is technological. The same move therefore changes income, habits and tools at once.

Culture shapes how policy lands. A rule written for cities may fail where language or trading customs differ, such as market days or seasonal farming. A firm that maps local customs before opening will face less resistance and sell more.

Technology now moves fastest of all. A new app can change how buyers pay, while a rival's machine can cut costs quickly. Firms that watch tools but ignore habits keep one eye closed, because buyers still decide with their customs and incomes.
In Nigeria, power and data costs also shape technology, so a tool that works in a city may pause in a rural town during outages.
A student who names one surrounding only will miss the pull of the rest, so revision should map each event to two or three surroundings before answering.
bullets: A levy can be political, economic and technological at once
Customs decide whether a city rule works in a village market
Payment apps change tools, but habits still decide adoption
Managers who watch one surrounding alone will miss the rest

content.heading: Go deeper: Safe products, philanthropy and societal consideration
paragraphs: Safe products need standards that buyers cannot see. A loaf may look fine yet carry excess preservative, so agencies test samples and firms label contents. Labelling that states ingredients honestly lets buyers choose and lets honest firms win.

Philanthropy and responsibility differ in motive and reach. Giving books is voluntary and costs the giver, while fair wages and safe waste handling are owed because the firm profits from the community. A firm can give generously yet still pollute, so giving alone never proves responsibility.

Societal consideration turns neighbours into early decision makers. A firm that visits fishing groups before siting a plant learns about spawning seasons and sacred sites in time to adjust. That early talk is cheaper than a protest, a ban or a court case.
In a Nigerian market, that logic explains why a trusted brand can charge more: safety and fairness are product features, not charity added after the sale.
bullets: Standards and honest labels make safety visible to buyers
Philanthropy is voluntary; responsibility is owed daily
A generous firm can still be irresponsible if it pollutes
Early neighbour talk is cheaper than protest or court

content.heading: Go deeper: Water, air and land pollution in the Delta
paragraphs: In the Niger Delta, oil spills start from equipment failure, sabotage or ageing lines. Crude floats on creeks, sinks into mud and coats mangrove roots, so fishing and farming lose their base. The same spill can therefore be water, land and air harm at once.

Air pollution hides in flares and smoke that season. Gas flares burn day and night, warming air and spreading soot over homes, while traffic and generators add fine particles. Acid rain that follows can sour soils and tin roofs, a cost rarely billed to the emitter.

For business, the bill arrives as fines, clean-up duties and lost trust. Firms that handle waste badly may save money today but face bans, compensation and empty jetties tomorrow. Cleaning a creek costs more than preventing the spill, which is why prevention carries the exam mark.
The lesson for revision is simple: name the medium first, then the business cost, because examiners score the link from pollution type to firm and community loss.
bullets: Crude on creeks and mud harms water and land together
Flares, smoke and traffic add air pollution and soot
Fines, clean-up and lost trust follow badly handled waste
Prevention costs less than cleaning a polluted creek
